                                         Part 1.—Brief Description of the Province.

        3. Interest of the Punjab to the Sociologist.—To the student of religion and sociology the Province
   presents features of'peculiar interest. In the earliest days of Hinduism the people of the Panjab Proper
   were a byeword in the mouths of the worshippers of Brahma, and Brahminism has always been weaker
   there than perhaps in any other part of India. Neither Islam nor the Hindu religion has ever been able to
   expel from the lives of the people the customs and superstitions which they brought with them from the
   homes of their ancestors ; and the worship of godlings unknown to the Hindu pantheon, the social cus-
   toms which still survive in full force among the majority of the nominal adherents of either religion, and
   the peculiar cults of the inferior and outcast races, offer for investigation an almost virgin field full of the
   richest promise. In the hills the Hindu religion and the caste-system to which it gave birth are to be
   found free in a very unusual degree from alteration by external influences, though doubtless much deteriorat-
   ed by decay from within. Sikhism must be studied in the Panjab if at all, and among the Bishnois of
   Hariina is to be found a curious offshoo.t from the national religion which is peculiar to them alone. For
   the inquiry into primitive institutions and the early growth of property in land the Panjab affords material
   of singular completeness and importance. Tribal organisation and tenures are to be found nowhere in
   India in such primitive integrity as on the western frontier of the Province, while in its eastern plains the
   village communities are typically perfect in their development. Between the two extremes ever)- step in
   the gradation from one form to the other is exemplified, while in the hills of Kangra and Simla community
   of rights, whether based on the tribe or on the village, is unknown.
        The Panjab can show no vast cities to rival Calcutta and Bombay, no great factories, no varied
   mineral wealth ; but the occupations of its people are still not without an interest of their own, The
   husbandmen of the Panjab furnish to the English market supplies of wheat already considerable and yearly
   increasing in magnitude.     The pursuits of the nomad pastoral tribes of the western doubs and of the
   river populations of the Indus and Satluj, the Pawi'ndah traffic of the Derajat, and the salt mines of Jahlam
   are .all well worthy of investigation and description ; while the silk and pashm fabrics and embroideries of
   Dehli, Peshawar, Ludhianah and Amritsar, the enamels of Multan, the damascening of Sialkot and Gnjrat,
   the pottery of Peshawar and Multan, and the beautiful jewellery and miniature painting of Dehli, have
   acquired a fame extending far beyond the limits of the Province.
         4. Boundaries and Administrative Divisions.—-The Panjab Proper, together with Kashmir which
    lies to its north, occupies the extreme north-western corner of India. Along its northern borders run the
    Himalayas which divide it from Kashmir. To its west and north-west lies Afghanistan, from which it is
    separated on the west by the Suleman Mountains, and on the north-west by the ranges which run I rom the
    eastern extremity of the Safed Koh north-east to join the Himalavas and south-west to meet the Sule-
    mans. To the south lies the great Rajputana desert, in which indeed is included a large part of Bahawal-
    pur; while to the east the river Jamna divides the Panjab from the NorthAYest Provinces.
          In shape the Province is something between a dice-box and an hour-glass, the axes crossing at Lahore

       5. The Panjab includes two classes of territory : that belonging to the British Crown, and that in the
 possession of the thirty-six feudatory chiefs of the Province, almost all of whom pay tribute in some form
 or other, and all of whom are subject to a more or less stringent control exercised by the Local Govern-
 ment. The area of British territory is 106,632 square miles and its population 18,850.437; ihc corre-
 sponding figures for the collective Native States, excluding Kashmir of which no census ha^ been taken on
 the present occasion, are 35.817 and 3,861,683. British territory is divided into thirty-two districts which
 are grouped under ten divisions, and each of which except the sanitarium of Simla comprises as large an
 area and population as can conveniently be controlled from its head-quarters. The dominions of the thirty-
 six native chiefs vary in size from the principalities of Patiala and Bahawalpur, with areas of 6,000 and
  15,000 square miles and populations of 1,500,000 and 600,000 respectively and ruled over by chi(.-ls sub-
 ject only to the most general supervision, to the tiny state of Dadhi with an area of one square mile and a
  total population of 170 souls whose ruler is independent in little more than the name.
       6. The Himalayan Tract.—Along the eastern portion of our northern border, and within the great
 net-work of mountain ranges which fringe the central system of the Himalayas, are situated the states of
 Ohamba, Mandi, and Suket, together with Nahan, Bashahr, and the twenty smaller states which are under
 the charge of the Superintendent of Hill States at Simla ; while among them lie the hill station of Simla
 and the great Kangra District, the latter including the Kulu valley which stretches up to the mighty range
 of the mid-Himalayas, and the cantons of Lahul and Spitf which, situated beyond the mid-Himalayas,
 belong geographically to Ladakh and Tibet rather than to India. This mountainous tract includes an
 area of some 19,840 square miles much of which is wholly uninhabited, and a scanty population of about
  I
    »539'°°° souls living scattered about the remaining area in tiny hamlets perched on the hill-sides or
 nestling in the valleys, each surrounded by its small patches of terraced cultivation, irrigated from the
 streams which run down every gulley or fertilised by the abundant rainfall of the hills.
       The people chiefly consist of hill Rajputs, including Thakars, R At his, and RaVats. and of Kanets,
  Ghirats., BraTimans, and the DAgis or menials of the hills. They are, either by origin or by long isolation
  from their neighbours of the plains, very distinct from the latter in most respects ; and they speak dialects
  peculiar to the hills, though belonging to the Hindi group except in the trans-Himalayan cantons where
 -Tibetan is spoken. They are almost exclusively Hindus, but curiously strict as regards some and lax as
  regards others of the ordinances of their religion. The nature of the country prevents the growth of
   large towns, trade is confined to the little that crosses the high passes which lead into Tibet, and the
  people are almost wholly rural, supplementing the yield of their fields by the produce of numerous flocks
   of sheep and goats, and by rude home manufactures with which they occupy themselves during the long

 are numerous in Ambala and Karnad, Tagas in Karnal and Dehli> Ahfrs in Rohtak, Dehli and Gurgaon,
 and Meos and Khanzadahs in Gurgaon.
        15. The Hissar district to the south of the tract differs from the districts just mentioned chiefly in
 that, lying as it does on the confines of Bikaner, the dialect and people are more akin to those of Raj-
 putana than to those of .Hindustan, Rajputs being very numerous, and there being a considerable Ahfr
 population. The religion ^is still Hindu, with a certain admixture of a curious sect called Bishnoi. The
 Sirsa district which forms the western portion of the southern border of the tract was all but uninhabited
 till it came under English rule; and it has drawn its settlers pretty equally from Hindu and Hindi-speaking
 Hissar and Rajputana and from the Sikh and PanjAbi-speaking Jat state of Patiala, while its western
 portion is occupied by Mahomedan immigrants from the lower Satluj.
        16. In all the remainder of the tract Panjabi is the language of the people. Immediately below the
 hills Sikhism has obtained but little hold, and the Hindu element, strong in Hushyarpur, gradually gives
 way to the Musalman as we pass westwards through Gurdaspur till it fades into comparative insignifi-
  cance in Sialkot. But all the centre of the tract, the great Phulkiam states of Patiala, Jind and Nabha,
  the states of Faridkot and Malerkotla, and the districts of Ludhianah, Firozpur, Lahore and Amritsar,
  and in a less degree of Jalandhar and Kapurthala, form the very centre and stronghold of the Panjab Sikhs.
  Even here however a very large proportion of the population is Musalman, a proportion constantly
  increasing from east to west; and it is the Hindu element alone which is displaced by the Sikh. In the
  matter of race the population of this portion of the tract is very uniform, Rajputs, Jats, Gujars, and their
  allied tribes forming the staple of the agricultural population, largely supplemented hy their attendant
  menials. Among the Siwaliks and immediately under the hills Jats are few and Rajputs and Ghirats
  numerous, while somewhat further south the proportion of Jats increases and Gujars, Sainis and A rains,
  and in Kapurthala Kambohs, Mahtams, and Dogars, become important elements in the population. In the
  Lahore Division, Faridkot, and the Phulkian states the mass of the population is Jat; though in Lahore,
  Firozpur, and Faridkot, Kambohs and Mahtams, and in Firozpur Dogars hold large areas, while in
  Patiala, jind and Nabha there is a considerable admixture of Ahfrs. The Changars and Sansis of Amrit-
  sar and the surrounding districts, the BaAvarias of the Upper Satluj, the Rawals of the northern districts
  and Lahore, and the Aheris of the Hissar division are curious outcast tribes, some of them probably
  aboriginal; and as we pass westwards and northwards from Hindustan and Rajputana into the Piovince,
  the Banya of the Dehli Territory gives place to the Khatri of the central, the Si'id of the northern, and the
  Arora of the western Panjab.
        17. The tract includes all the most fertile, wealthy, and populous portions of the Province, and may be
 called the gntRaTy~ef'^fe€-Tp-anjib. Within it lie the three great cities of Dehli, Amritsar, and Lahore, besides
_&--very large proportion of the I?~fg"er town?; and the population is by comparison with that of the western
 Panjab largely urban. Trade and manufactures nourish, ".'bile with the exception of the south-westward
 portions where flocks and herds pasture in extensive jungles, the greater part of the culturable area is
 under the plough.
        18. The Western Plains.—The great plains lying to the west of the Lahore meridian present a strik-
 ing contrast to those to the east of that line. They form the common terminus of the two Indian monsoons,
 which have exhausted themselves of their vapour before they reach their goal ; and the rainfall, heaviest in
  the north and east and decreasing towards the west and south, is everywhere so scanty that cultivation
  without irrigation is absolutely impossible, But in this very circumstance they find their security against
  famine or distress from drought; for their cultivation is almost independent of rain, a failure of which means
  little worse than a scarcity of grass, in itself a sufficiently serious calamity1. In many parts, indeed, more
  danger is to be anticipated from excessive floods than from deficient rainfall. The tract is traversed
  throughout its length by five great rivers, the Satluj, RaVi, Chanab, Jahlam, and Indus; and along either
  side of each of these runs at a distance of a few miles a more or less distinctly marked bank, which de-
   fines the excursions of the river within recent times as it has shifted from side to side in its course. These
  banks include between them strips of low-lying land which are periodically inundated by the rising floods
   as the winter snows of the Himalayas melt under the summer sun, or in which the nearness of the subsoil
   water makes well-irrigation easy. All outside these narrow boundaries is a high arid plain. Bevond the
   Indus, and between the Satluj and the Jahlam and its continuation in the Chanab, it consists of soil which,
   wherever water is available, is sufficiently fertile save where north of the Satluj that saline efflorescence
   which has so puzzled geologists clothes the surface for mites together like a recent fall of snow. But bet-
   ween the Indus and the Jahlam-Chanab and south of the Satluj it is covered by great parallel lines of
   rolling sand separated by narrow hollows in which the original soil is exposed.
         19. The Gujranwala and Wazirabad tahslls of the Gujranwala district 3 secure a fair amount of rain
   by their vicinity to the hills. Numerous streams, for the most part of intermittent flow, which run down
   from the Suleman Mountains to join the Indus, and innumerable small inundation canals carried out from
   the Satluj, the lower Chanab, the upper Jahlam, and the lower Indus across the zone of well-irrigation
    into the edges of the central steppes render cultivation possible along their courses ; while wells sunk in
    the long hollows of the thai or sandy desert and the drainage of the bar or stiff loam uplands collected in
       1
          Rain, of course, is needed, here as elsewhere. Rut its absence means only a diminished yield, and not none at all ; and so little is
  sufficient if the fall comes at the right time, and absolute drought occurs so seldom, that the crops may be said never to fail from this
  Cause.

                                  Part II.—Short Account of the Census Operations.




                      PART II-SHORT ACCOUNT OF THE CENSUS OPERATIONS.

       27. Previous enumerations of the people.—The present is the third Census that has been taken
 of the population of British Territory in the Pan jab, the people having been numbered on the 1st January
 18551, on the 10th January 1868, and now on the 17th February 1881. In the Native States, on the other
hand, nothing further than a more or less rough estimate of the population had ever been attempted before
the present Census. I believe I am safe in saying that the present enumeration is more accurate than either
of those which preceded it; and it is at least certain that the directions issued, the system followed, and the
supervision exercised, were far more elaborate and descended to much greater minuteness of detail on
the present than on any previous occasion. In 1855 no preliminary record was prepared, the enumeration
being begun and ended on the night of the Census itself; while neither in 1855 nor in 1S68 was' any
attempt made to record particulars separately for each person enumerated. On both these occasions the
enumerator merely ascertained from the head of the house how many children, youths, and adults of each sex
were sleeping under his roof, whether as members of the family or as visitors, the numbers thus ascer-
tained were entered in the appropriate columns, and all members of the same family were assumed to have
the same religion, caste, and occupation. It needs but small acquaintance with the people of the
country to be able to appreciate the additional accuracy which has been attained by making a separate
entry with name and full details for each individual. Moreover, at the present Census many particulars
have been recorded to ascertain which no attempt had previously been made ; and especially age, tribal
sub-divisions, and occupations have been stated in much more minute detail than ever before. The
classification of entries of caste and occupation was, in 1868, made in the district offices in accordance
with brief instructions of a very general nature ; and it is hardly possible that this work, which in the present
Census I have found to be by far the most difficult and delicate part of the operations, should have been
performed with as much uniformity as has attended the present classification.
      28. General outline of the scheme of operations.—The scheme of operations of the present Census
was based upon the recommendations of a Committee appointed by the Government of India in 1877-78 to
consider the subject, largely modified in details by both the Imperial and the Local Government. The
successive steps in the operations may be summarised as follows :—
             (a) Division of the country into blocks, or units of enumeratipn."
             (6) Preparation of fists of houses and famDje^ a nd numbering of houses.
             (c) Selection of agency.^^_wW—•=—*—' ~
             {d) Prepa^atiQiiu-^-5 preliminary record of the population.
             {e) -^k-is thej^g itself; or the correction of the preliminary record so as to bring it into accordance
     -- « l c o n g i n #jfifiacts as they stood on the Census night.
 S
   J S Z i i ^ ) T h e abstracting of the entries in the Census Schedules.
             (g) The tabulation in detail of the figures thus abstracted.
             (h) The compilation of the final Census tables from the figures thus tabulated in detail.
These various operations are described and discussed in detail in Book II of the present Report, and the
exact meaning of each of the several units employed for Census purposes, such as the house, the family,
the village, and the town, is there precisely defined. There too will be found a description of the difficul-
ties we encountered with suggestions for their avoidance or abatement at a future Census, a discussion
of the degree of accuracy which the results may be held to possess, and detailed information as to the
attitude of the people towards the operations. It will be sufficient to give in this place such a general outline
of the method of Census as may enable the reader to understand how the results presently to be discussed
were arrived at.
      20. Demarcation of Census blocks.—The first thing done was to split up the Province into blocks
of such a size that a single man could conveniently visit all people living within any one of them on the
Census night. In the hill tracts indeed this was impossible, nor was it necessary to divide off the uninhabit-
ed and inaccessible sides of Himalayan Mountains. In such places it sufficed to allot to each enumerator so
many of the small scattered hamlets and isolated homesteads in which the hillmen live as he was able
to deal with. So again, in the great arid pasture lands of the Western Plains men were told off to
visit the camps of the nomad population, the exact position of which was ascertained from the tribal
headmen a few days beforehand. But throughout the remaining portion of the Panjab plains the whole
area was divided off into blocks, and a separate enumerator made responsible for the enumeration of all
persons found within the area of each on the night of the Census.
     30. Numbering of houses.—The next step was to make rough sketch maps of the towns, villages, and
hamletSj to prepare a list of the houses in each block and of the families in each house, and to paint
up on the walls of the houses the serial numbers which distinguished them on the maps and in the lists.
To any one unacquainted with Indian town and village life, and with the feeling of the people regarding
privacy and the seclusion of women, it will be impossible to realise the difficulty experienced in
answering the question—what is a house? In the hills and in parts of the western Panjab the peasant often
lives with his family in a separate house or hut built among his fields or by his well, or in one of a small
group of such separate houses which lie close together and constitute a hamlet. In such cases the
matter is simple enough. But the ground-plan of an ordinary Panjab village in the plains is often not
unlike one of those mazes with which the ingenuous English youth who believes in Fair Rosamond is
wont to delight himself. It is surrounded by a ditch and mud wall, and entered by one, two, or three gates

     ' T h e corresponding Census of the Dehli Territory, namely Dehli, Gurgaon, p.^rt of K a m a l . Hissar, and Rohtak, was taken under
the North-Western Provinces Government on ist January 1853; while the Census of Bhattidna or Sirsa was a settlement Census, taken
village by village between 1S52 and 1863.

  these 61,140 people no fewer than 45,082 were non-officials, of whom only 431 received payment. The
  remainder performed the duties assigned to them, often extending over a considerable period
  and always of an irksome and uninteresting nature, without compensation of any kind, or hope of reward
  beyond the presentation of a printed letter of thanks and the good-will of the authorities 1 . The cheerful
  readiness and interest with which the work was almost without exception undertaken and carried through
  by this unpaid agency, speak most strongly for the good and willing feeling of the people.
        36. The Preliminary Record.—Having mapped out the work before them, selected the agency, and
  put the enumerators through a short course of practical instruction, the officers in charge began with the
  new year the preparation of the preliminary record which was, after such few corrections as subsequent
  births, deaths, and movements of the people might render necessary on the Census night, to represent the
  result of the whole operations. This record might in fact almost be called the Census itself. The
  village population is essentially a stationary one, the alterations made in the entries, on the night of
  the Census were comparatively unimportant, and on the care and accuracy with which the preliminary record
  was tilled in practically depended the whole value of the results. It was made and corrected at leisure
  during January 1881 ; and during the greater part of that month the Census staff was busily employed
  in its preparation, the enumerators going round their blocks from house to house recording "the
  required particulars for each person, and the superior officers riding about from village to village and from
  block to block, inspecting, testing, correcting and encouraging. Much patient care was required of
  them. The details to be recorded were numerous, and the instructions of necessity often failed to meet
  local peculiarities; while the habitual inaccuracy natural to uninstructed minds, the tendency of the
  inferior castes to extenuate their present status by claiming an origin of fabulous glory, and the convic-
  tion so rooted in the native breast that if the Government asks him what is his sect, or otherwise, it is his
  business to have a sect, or otherwise, or, if he has hitherto been unaware that he possesses one, to invent
  one on the spot for the satisfaction of his superiors,—all tended to make the attainment of a really
  accurate record dependent upon the exercise of tact, patience and perseverance. Add to this the hopeless
  imbecility of some of the enumerators, the utter illegibility of their handwriting, and the impossibility
  of finding better men, and it is not to be wondered at that in many instances the preliminary record
  was practically prepared by the supervisor rather than by the enumerator.
         37. Where, as was often the case, the supervisor was the village accountant, this was far the best
  course that could possibly be followed ; and I am inclined to recommend, for reasons fully stated in a sub-
  sequent chapter, that at a future Census the preliminary record of the villages be wholly prepared by these
   men. I have already noticed the danger of enumeration by men of a certain degree of education, and
  the supervising staff were not wholly exempt from the same defect. Many even who shoujd have known better
  did much harm by what they called "aiming at uniformity.'-' - Now the'only uniformity that exists anions
  the people of the Panjab is the uniform absence-of uniformity. In this way a Master-of-Arts of the Calcutta
   University spoiled the lanpcyags-returns for the tract under his charge by entering as the mother-tongue of
  the people, not >vr;aL Wey called their languages, but what he called them ; justifying his action by a learned
   exE&sitKJiTof^cn^ affinities of the local dialects, which would have been very useful had he merely based it upon
* the entries made by the people, instead of altering those entries to suit his theories. So an English officer of
  high standing took upon himself to omit a portion of the information called for, because it was in his opinion
  unimportant. At the same time, it is very difficult to draw the line between blindly recording whatever the
  people choose to state and pragmatically refusing to accept their statements because they conflict with a
  preconceived theory. Of the two the former is by far the smaller evil. But in some cases it is impossible
  to accept the statements made. When a lusty male in the prime of manhood tells you that he is 15 years old,
  or a tottering elder that his winters number " 20 or 30," it is necessary to exercise your own judgment in the
   matter. So, when an oilman says that he is a Mughal or a Rajput he may be so in reality, and it is most
   unsafe to assume that because he is an oilman he therefore cannot be telling the truth. But if he is one of
   a community of Telis (the ordinary oilman caste) and marries among Telis, and is and always has been known
   to his neighbours as a Teli, his assertion is but vain-glorying and must be rejected. And this is the chief
   reason why I think that the preliminary record, which is the very backbone of the Census, should be pre-
   pared as far as possible by the village accountants who live among the people, and know every man,
   woman and child in the village.
         38. The completion of the preliminary record was followed by a pause, which was employed in making
   arrangements for the enumeration of prisoners, dispensary patients, gangs of workmen, travellers by boat,
   rail and road, and other similar floating populations.
         39. The Census itself.—A couple of days before the 17th of February, the supervisors visited their
   blocks to assure themselves that all the enumerators were at their posts with the completely tested record
    in readiness, and to distribute the red ink which has to be used for alterations and additions made on the
    Census night. Proclamations were issued to the people requesting them as far as possible to stay at
    home after nightfall on the 17th, not to go to bed till the enumerator had visited them, and till then to
    keep a lamp burning. During the day time of the 17th the nomad grazing camps of the Western Plains were
    visited, and the Census was taken in some of the more mountainous tracts where the snow and the diffi-
    cult nature of the country made a night visitation impossible. But the great mass of the population was enu-
    merated by moonlight. Evening brought the husbandmen and cowherds home from the held and pastures ;
    and as soon as night fell and the lamps were lit, the enumerators, accompanied by the village headmen
    and by men carrying torches, started on their rounds. As a rule they found the head of the family wait-
    ing at the door with a lamp in his hand to receive them. They read out to him the entries in the schedules,
    cut out such persons as had died or gone away, entered those who had been born or come to the house in the
    interval, and passed on to the next house. In the Kulu hills Mr. Anderson ingeniously numbered his houses
    down hill; and the enumerator, climbing at painful leisure to the top of his block during the day, quietly
    gravitated to the bottom after nightfall, calling at each house on his way. About 6 o'clock next morning

       40. The attitude of the people.—The attitude of the people was admirable throughout. Occa-
sionally an ill-conditioned fai/ir or sulky shopkeeper or a nasty-tempered old woman would resent
the inquiries made of them, and use exceedingly improper language to the enumerator who was
questioning them. And on the Census night itself I was appealed to by an enumerator in difficulties,
and spent half an hour in listening to abuse of the English Government in general and myself in
particular from a sleepy Banya who, roused from his warm bed which he had sought too early, sat
shivering on the doorstep and discussing each question before he answered it at most unneces-
sary length. But on the whole the people looked on with amused curiosity at the trouble and
fuss that Government was making about the filling up of a set of useless forms. Of course there
were the usual rumours current among the lower and more ignorant classes and in the more backward
tracts. The Government inquired for the first time into the number of families, and was therefore about to
revive the obsolete hearth-tax; and some of the Hushyarpur Giijars went so far as to break up their hearths
on the day before the Census. It recorded sex and age, and so wanted soldiers for its Kabul campaign
and young wives for its soldiers, in so much that in one place the people hurriedly wedded their marriageable
girls to save them from impressment. It demanded particulars about occupation, and had not a license-tax
been recently imposed? It recorded each person where he or she was found on the Census night, and hus-
bands recalled their wives from their father-in-laws' houses lest they should lose their marital rights.
In some cases there was a tendency to conceal the existence of old persons and infants, whom it would
obviously have been unfair to tax; and in a tract in Peshawar which had suffered much from drought, the
people thought that Government was going to give them relief based upon the number of mouths, and
were inclined to show a quite phenomenal increase of population. The Spiti peopled petitioned to be allow-
ed to collect in one place, there to have their numbers taken. Some rumours were less obviously natural;
as, for instance, that search was being made for a lost child of Her Majesty, or for the eternal Im3m Mahdi;
that Government were about to transfer a portion of the Bengal and Madras populations to thePanjab; that
rain was not allowed to fall till the Census was over lest it should wash off the house numbers; and that
numbering the people was unlucky, and the deaths which followed the preliminary record due to this
 cause. But these misunderstandings were not general, and soon passed away; in fact many of them were
only raised to be laughed at. The gray beards remembered two previous Censuses without any evil effects
following upon them, all the leading men took part in the operations, the people were accustomed to statis-
tical inquiries in connection with the revenue, and almost every district report bears strong testimony to
the cheerfuJ alpciiiy with which they entered into the spirit of the thing, rendered all the assistance in tfieir
 power, and endured the repeated inquiries of enumerator, supervisor, and- superint*^ent without murmur-
 ing, and to the real anxiety they displayed that the information recorded should be'"aSj£lfc2££- " Cherisher
 of the poor, " said an old man to Mr. Coldstream," all my household has been correctly enumerated^'^inp-'li?--"'—
 one goat. " An old lady followed another District Officer about for some days because she averred that :he
 had not been entered in the schedules. Especially the prohibition against the employment of the rank an i
 tile of the Police in the enumeration, and against asking the names of women where there was any objection
 to stating them, gave great satisfaction and convinced the people that their prejudices had been considered
 and that no harm was intended. Out of the 19,000,000 of people enumerated in British Territory only 5
 were proceeded against criminally for refusing to answer questions, and these all in a single district.
     41. The Comedy of "Census".—Avery curious illustration of the feelings of the people on the subject
was afforded by an original comedy entitled " Census," which was performed at Lahore for several nights
in succession to crowded houses by a strolling company of Parsis. I went to see it, and enjoyed it im-
mensely. It was really comic, and the fun, if occasionally a little broad, was absolutely good-humoured
throughout. The impressment of the enumerator, his delight at becoming a servant of Government, his
dismay at finding that he was to receive no pay, his zeal in reducing others to a like plight with himself; the
terror of the Banya, and especially of his wife, at the rumour that the numbers of the sexes were to be
equalised by killing the spare men and the percentages of infirm corrected by making more where neces-
sary, their resolve to fly into the jungles till the tyranny should be overpast, their horror at hearing the
enumerator's demand for admittance, the awe with which they listened to his account of his powers and
 the way in which they were to be exercised, their anxiety to assuage him with sweetmeats, and his
greediness and self-importance ; the meeting of enumerators on the Census night, how one had entered al)
 the living things in his block, flies included (an estimate merely), how another had counted unborn babes
 as half a child each, and how a third had come away from the hospital with blank schedules because all the
 patients had died ; and the final scene in the forest where all the enumerators in turn make love to the
 Banya's wife, till Tahsildar ji appears, examines their books and consigns them all to gaol,—such were the
 main features of a very amusing piece, played with considerable comic power, and intensely enjoyed by
 the audience.
       Nor were comic incidents wholly absent from the actual operations. A Magistrate successfully justi-
 fied his having entered a village pond as an inhabited house, by explaining to me that a fogir was stand-
 ing up to his waist in the water and declared his intention of remaining there till after the Census ; one
 enumerator came near having his head broken for putting, as in duty bound, the prescribed series of ques-
 tions to an irascible villager, which involved asking him whether his mother was married; while another
 who spoke English stigmatised the female adults of his block as adulteresses.

 approximately correct. The figures for religion are probably as accurate as those for sex, if each man's
 account of his own religion be accepted as true; but I shall show in the chapter on religion that it is
  often exceedingly difficult for a Native to say, or for anybody else to discover, what his religion really is.
. There are Hindus and Hindus, Musalimins and Musalmdns, Sikhs and Sikhs, and the figures must be taken
  subject to limitations which I shall do my best to indicate in treating of the subject. The figures for civil
  condition I take to be correct on the whole, though it is just possible that girls of an age at which tribal
  custom requires them to be married may have been in some cases so returned, though really single, while
  concubines may not unseldom have been shown as wives. The entries for occupations err from vague-
  ness or incompleteness rather than from positive inaccuracy. The division of labour is far less clearly de-
  fined in India than in Europe, while too often general terms have been used where more precise ones
  might properly have been employed. Many hereditary callings embrace several occupations, and have
 been interpreted to mean one of them in one place and another in another; and the English equivalents
 given in the occupation tables require much explanation and limitation, and should often be taken as
  indications rather than as exact descriptions of the occupations to which the figures refer. The subject is
  discussed at length in the chapter on occupations. The figures for education and infirmities are probably
  fairly accurate, save that respectable women, though they may read, are not supposed, in some parts of
  the Province at least, to be able to write; and this prejudice may have affected the educational statistics
  for females. The details of language are probably as accurate as circumstances will allow, for with
  several of our Panjab tongues their affinities are so close and the intermediate forms of dialect so
  numerous, that it is as impossible to draw hard-and-fast lines and to say, this is a species or language
  and that a variety or dialect, as it is to draw the corresponding distinction in the case of birds or butteflies.
  Birthplace, where indicating difference of race or actual immigration, has I believe been returned with
  great accuracy; but it is probable that accidental birth in another district or province has often been
  forgotten, while the figures for the birthplaces of gipsy and vagrant tribes can hardly be relied upon.
        47. As for caste, opinions will probably differ as to the correctness of the results. My own belief is that
  the Census record gave us a very true representation of the distribution of tribes and castes, and that the
  errors were quite unimportant in amount as regards the main divisions at any rate, and were chiefly con-
  fined to those minor sub-divisions which are of comparatively small significance. But, as already explained,
  the entries in that record had to undergo an elaborate process of classification and assortment before they
  were finally reduced to the form which they assume in the tables; and in our present state of ignorance as
  to the tribal distribution and divisions of the people, it is certain that I must have erred over and over
  again in my attempts to marshal the facts and figures. It is probable however that these errors do not
  materially affect the general grouping of the people under the main tribal heads, and it is to be hoped that
  the material we have now collected will be examined at leisure before the next Census, and that in 1891 we
  shall be in a position to deal far more effectively and certainly with the entries of tribe and caste. The
  subject is the largest and most difficult of all those with which I have to deal, and I must refer the reader
  for a full discussion of it to the chapter on caste. I have prefixed to each chapter of the report a short
  examination of the figures-with which it deals, in which I have endeavoured to mdicalc ,!Q.>Y far they may
  be accepted as trustworthy ; and I am of opinion that the errors,-save in a very 'ew cases         . ^~^^a^e-
  prominently drawn attention in discussing the actual entries, are absolutely in?it"nificant"Vri~ comparison
  with the numbers involved.
      48. The cost of the Census, direct and indirect.—To put a plain truth in homely language, the Census
 was an unmitigated nuisance to all concerned; and from October 1880 to February 1881 I was probably
 the best abused man in the Panjab. The operations threw a great deal of extra labour upon a staff which
 was already overworked without any hope of additional remuneration, they took men away from their
 ordinary duties which naturally fell into arrears to be cleared off afterwards, and they temporarily dis-
 turbed the whole routine of district administration. But they were exceptional in their nature, Govern-
 ment attached great importance to their being successfully carried through, and the whole Panjab staff
 laid aside all other duties that could be neglected for a time with safety, threw their whole heart into the
 Census work, and willingly and zealously, and in my opinion successfully, strove to ensure a satisfactory
 result. The cost of the Census has been about Ri,45,ooo, which may be roughly distributed as follows :—

 But of this sum R20,ooo were paid to the Central Jail for work which could have been done at far lower
 rates elsewhere, the difference going into the pockets of Government.
      The cost was kept down to this low figure in two ways : first, by freely utilising the official staff, to the
 hindrance of other work; and secondly, by calliijg in to our aid a large body of non-official and unpaid
 helpers. Thus the enumeration cost Government nothing but the price of the printing and paper, and a
 sum of Ri6,ooo, which was distributed after the work was over to those private individuals who had helped
 most zealously. Some few officers have criticised more or less severely the policy which, as they say, dis-
 located the general administration of the Province and threw an irksome burden upon the shoulders of a
 considerable section of the community, in order to save Government a few thousands of rupees, and to obtain
 by forced labour what should have been paid for, and was worth paying for if it was worth doing at all.
 They point out that a result quite as accurate, for all purposes of practical administration, could have been
                                                                                                      13
Para. 49- "1                                    INTRODUCTORY.
Chap. I . J

                            Part II.—Short Aecount of the Census Operations.

obtained without entailing either of these evils, by following a less elaborate procedure and by collecting
less minute and varied information.
      49. Answer to criticisms.—'Now the injury done to the administration of the Province may be
summed up in two words : settlement operations were somewhat hindered, and the village returns of crop
areas, mutations, and the like, were in many cases prepared either hurriedly or not at all. The hindrance to
settlement operations was practically a matter of money : Government paid men to do Settlement and employ-
ed them in doing Census. The annual papers no doubt suffered, though they were prepared without diffi-
culty in some districts, and I doubt whether the Census was always really responsible for all that was iaid at
its door; but even if once in every ten years the annual papers were omitted altogether, I do not know
that any very grievous results would ensue. Other minor hindrances no doubt occurred ; but the above are
I believe the only two of any importance, and I do not think they constitute a very weighty indictment
against the Census. As for the policy of calling upon the people to aid in their own enumeration, 1 am
wholly opposed to the strictures which have been passed upon it. The Natives are far too apt to look upon
" the sarkar " as something entirely outside themselves whose business it is to do things for them ; and I
think that the lesson of self-help, "slight as it was, which their taking their own Census conveyed, and the
experience of joining with the officials to secure a given end, even if that end was one the value of which
they were unable fully to appreciate, were altogether healthy and wholesome. There are numberless
indications in the district reports that, where tact and patient influence were exerted, a real and genuine
interest in the proceedings was created among the people, and that the body of helpers, even where a
little unwilling at the first, gradually did rise to something like an appreciation of the objects of Govern-
ment and to an intelligent pride in their own exertions. The matter was a small one and the effect tem-
porary" but so far as it went it was in my opinion wholly good.
      50. Moreover I do not see how the end contemplated could have been attained in any other way
than that adopted. Supposing that Government had been prepared to use none of the existing official staff
and to call in no private aid, and to do the whole work by a specially paid agency, and supposing, which
 I much doubt, that that agency had been forthcoming in sufficient number; 1 believe not only that the
 results would not have been worth the paper they were written on, but also that the people would have
suffered far more at the hands of a set of unscrupulous writers, the smallness of whose pay and the tem-
 porary nature of whose employment would have rendered impossible any effective check upon their
extortions, than they did by being called upon to exert themselves for a time and to do the work them-
selves. It is in my opinion precisely because the existing revenue staff, already familiar with statistical
inquiry-and intimately acquainted with the district and the people, were employed to take the Census,
because it was felt that the work had to be done without paid agency and that special efforts were
therefore necessary, because the natural leaders of the people and a considerable proportion of the people
themselves were enlisted- for the purpose, and because the Census was taken, not by a city man with
white clothes and an, itching palm, but by the accountant and the shop-keeper from the next village
supervised by tr*^ headman "of the circle, that results of such accuracy have been obtained and so little
dissatistacti^—^fjused.
     *5TTTKe~ criticism That more simple and less accurate results could have been obtained with smaller
friction and would have answered all practical purposes, is more difficult to answer. It is possible that
a less elaborate schedule would have sufficed ; that, for instance, in the present state of registration of
births and deaths detailed statistics of age, even if attainable with any degree of accuracy, are unneces-
sary. But if a Census is to be taken at all a column more or less to be rilled up makes but little difference,
or at any rate only affects the cost of tabulation ; and if one lesson rather than another is more and more
strongly impressed on the mind by successive years of Indian service, it is that in the matter of accuracy all
compromise is impossible. If absolute accuracy is insisted on, and every possible precaution taken to
secure it, a very high degree of accuracy will be attained; but if any license is allowed, and if it appears
that approximate results will be accepted, there is no limit to the slovenliness and error that will ensue.
A.Census was necessary, and if it was to be done at all it was worth doing well. It has been done, and I
believe that it"has been on the whole well done.
      52. The value Of the results.—It must always be remembered that the present Census was, so far as
 the Panjab is concerned, almost a first experiment. Previous enumerations of the people had been made ;
 but nothing on the same scale—nothing approaching the elaboration and minuteness of the present inquiry
 had ever before been attempted. There was nothing to guide me or the high, authorities under whom I
 worked in elaborating the scheme of operations ; and every contingency had as far as possible to be
 foreseen and provided for without the light of previous experience. Next to nothing was known about the
 divisions and occupations of the people, and the very extent of our ignorance was still to be discovered.
  I do believe that the facts set forth in the present report will substantially increase our acquaintance with
  the people of the Province, and that they include much that is valuable, and that if not really new, has
  at least never before been collected and arranged systematically for the whole Panjab. But I look upon
  the value and importance of the present Census as consisting, not so much in the results which have been
  obtained as in the experience which has been collected ; not so much in the additions that have been
- made to our knowledge as in the light which has been thrown upon our ignorance. We now partly
  perceive in what respects our knowledge is most defective, and we have a clearer idea than before of the
  best way to remedy its defects. Errors have been mdMe without number, and it will be my duty to point
  them out in every chapter of the report. But at least we know to a great extent where we have failed,
  and can point out the pitfalls which must be avoided in future. This is the object which I have kept
  in mind throughout while writing the report; to clear the way for the next Census, and to point out to
  the reader lines of inquiry which can meanwhile be followed with advantage.

results which have been obtained. To each chapter I shall- prefix a short description of the figures to be

in which more detailed information may be found wilhbe a useful addition to that outline.
      Besides the paragraphs on the figures and on the bibliography, there will occur throughout the report
other amplifications or discussions of details, containing information which though useful does not form
part of the general thread of the report. All such paragraphs will be printed in,smaller type than the body
of the text in order the more clearly to mark their nature.
      The second book of the report will be devoted to a detailed description of the method followed in the
Census operations, and to suggestions for its improvement. I believe it will be of great value to the next
Panjib Census officer, and reference will often be made to it in discussing certain figures, for a description
of the manner in which they were obtained and of the significance which they therefore possess. But this
portion ot the report will possess no interest for the general reader, if such a person exist for an Indian
blue-book.

     68. Figures for England and the Panjab compared.—It so happens that the population of England
 and Wales at the Census of 1871 was 22,712,266, or only 146 souls more than the present population of
 the Panjab. This makes comparison easy. Abstract No. 5, which shows the distribution of the two
populations side by side, presents a very interesting contrast, and forcibly illustrates the remarks made
in paragraphs 62 and 63. Unfortunately the only volume of the English Census Report to which I have access
gives no figures for the populations of places under 2,000 inhabitants, no details of the number of small vil-
lages, and no definition of the line which has been drawn between the village and the town. It would
appear that all places of 2,000'inhabitants and no fewer than 139 places which did not reach that standard,
were classed as towns'. But all I can be certain of is that the number of places of 2,000 souls and over
is correctly given. I therefore give no 'details below that limit, and take the arbitrary standard of 5,000
souls as the demarcation between town and village. Thus the Panjab figures in the two Abstracts
Nos. 4 and 5 will not agree exactly.

      The extraordinary contrast between the distribution of the population' in the two countries is brought
out very strongly by these-figures. In the Panjib towns and villages of more than 5.000 inhabitants include
only 11'5 per cent, of the population; in England they include 56-i per cent, or nearly five times as
large a proportion. The corresponding percentages for towns and villages of over 2,000 souls are 26"o and
6i'2 respectively. On the other hand there are in the Panjab 1,195 villages of between 2,000 and 5,000
souls containing one-seventh of the population, against 358 such villages in England including one-twentieth
of the English population. Three-quarters of the people of the Panjab live in villages of under 2,000
inhabitants, while the corresponding proportion in England is just over three-eighths. In the Panjab we
have 52,870 towns and villages, of which more than half contain more than 200 souls and at least 41,000
are something more than mere hamlets; while in England and Wales there are only 15,416 "parishes,
townships, and places for which the population is separately returned," and this number must include very
many parishes which form parts only of towns.
      69. In order to make a comparison upon a more equal basis I have, in columns 9, 12, 15, and \S,
given the figures for the English population as it would stand if London and the other five cities of over
200,000 souls named in foot-note (6) to the abstract, to which-the Panjab can afford no sort of parallel, were
altogether excluded. So far as the total population is concerned this exclusion leaves the contrast only
slightly less striking than before. But it may be noticed in columns 7 to 12, which deal with the popula-
tion of towns of over 5,000 souls, that if we exclude the six great English cities, the largest towns contain
a much smaller proportion of the urban population in England than in the Panjab. This is only natural,
for .in both countries the two or three greatest cities include a population large beyond all comparison
with those immediately below them. The tendency of the large towns of the Province to increase
at the cost of the smaller ones, and of the general population to become more and more urban, is noticed
in the next chapter.

come last, the village is, as has already been explained, in the one case artificially large, and in the other
a mere hamlet. Excluding these we find Rohtak, with its great communities of Hindu Jats, far ahead of

      71 Conditions which determine the size of villages.—The causes which affect the size of villages
are many and various, but most prominent among them probably are, the degree in which order and secu-
rity have prevailed under the local Government, the tribal tenure of the land, the caste ot the cultivating
communities, and the physical character of the tract. The operation of these conditions has already been
indirectly indicated in paragraph 65.
      The state of the Province before it passed into our hands is broadly sketched in the next chapter.
Where as in the eastern and south-eastern districts, force had been for generations the only law and no
strong'rule had compelled respect for the life and property of others, the people were driven to hnd m
large and united village communities, such as we see in Rohtak, Hissar, Kama , and Dehi, the strength
and protection for which they looked in vain to their rulers; where on the other hand the S.kh rule was
strongest the cultivators naturally spread themselves more widely over their fields ; and accordingly the
central divisions of Lahore and Amritsar, and the Multan division which prospered under Sawan Mai, stand
low in the list.
      On the frontier anarchy was perhaps more rife than in any other portion of the Panjab ; but here the
tribal tenure interfered to modify the distribution of the population. Wherever the united tribe cr clan
held and cultivated under a strong tribal rule the tract which they occupied, the people, still semi-nomad in
 their habits, spread themselves widely over the country in small groups of two or three closely connected
 families having separate ownership in their cultivated lands and irrigation works, but with no clearly de-
 fined boundaries within the pastures common to the clan. But where the dominant race merely held the
 tract and left its cultivation to a subject population, we find the former collected in fortified villages of some
 considerable size, round which the latter, too poor to be the objects of assault, live scattered over their
 fields in small outlying hamlets. In both these cases however the village of our tables is, as explained 111
 paragraph 66, often purely artificial, and affords but little indication of the real distribution of the people.
                       22
                                                                THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE PEOPLE.                                                                                           r Para. 73.
                                                                                                                                                                                          L Chap. I I .

                                                Part I.—Distribution over Towns and Villages.

     The effect of the caste of the village-communities is closely allied to that of the conditions just dis-
cussed. It may be said broadly that the ruling races, such as Pathans, Biloches, Rajputs and Jats, have
almost a monopoly of large villages, not only because they alone had in former days wealth to protect, but
also because the inferior castes have as a rule obtained their property in land by being in the first instance
settled as small bodies of cultivators by the superior caste, or by the Government of the day. The Jats
especially have a tendency to form large communities living in single villages ; perhaps because they are of all
the Panjab races the most self-dependent and impatient of tribal control, so that the Jat village has to
find in its own strength the protection for which other castes look to the tribe 1 .
      Where again a fertile and easily worked soil, and still more where abundant irrigation or a plentiful
rainfall, renders cultivation easy and remunerative, the village has a tendency to be small, not only in area
but also in population ; while where a scanty rainfall and a limited supply of water made, when the tract
was first settled, a large area necessary for the rough and precarious cultivation, and especially for the nu-
merous flocks and herds which under these conditions supplement the produce of the fields, the communi-
ties are generally speaking large and powerful, for in such tracts not only is easy access to the fields of
less importance, but the people were in old days more addicted to prcedatory forays on a large scale, as
they still are to cattle-theft, and considerable strength was essential to the safety of the village. On the
other hand there is a further extreme, where the tract is so backward and the uncultivated lands so ex-
tensive that the latter have not been appropriated by any village ; and here grants of waste lands are
made to capitalists who settle small communities as pioneers of cultivation, or the pastoral inhabitants are
semi-nomad in their habits. In such cases the village proper has a tendency to be extremely small. I
have already described in paragraph 65 the condition which scatter the people of the hill-tracts so widely
over their area.
      72. I believe that were it possible to examine separately tracts in which these conditions are more or
 less constant, very striking figures might be adduced in' illustration of the operation of these influences.
 But the conditions vary so greatly from one part to another of the same district, the circumstances of the
 districts themselves diverge so widely, causes operating in opposite directions are so commonly present in
 the same tract, and the only figures available are based upon such very different data in different parts of
 the Province, that any detailed examination of them would be almost meaningless unless accompanied
 by very lengthy explanations. At the same time the following figures, while not actually proving any-
 thing, seem to lend support to the propositions advanced in the preceding paragraph. I have already
 explained the causes which, iri the Hill districts and to a less extent in the Multan and Derajat divisions,
 have too often rendered the "village" of our tables a purely artificial unit. Excluding on this ground Simla,
  Kangra, the two Derahs, Bannu, iVIultan, and Montgomery, and dividing the remaining 25 districts into
  5 croups according to the order of magnitude of their average village populations in which they stand in
  Abstract No. 6, we get the following averages for the respective groups:—

 The percentage of dominant races is unduly raised in the 4th group by the large percentage (64) of so-
 called Pathans in the hilly district of Hazara, and in the 5th group by the high percentage (44) of jats and
 Rajputs in Sirsa, which has only been settled within the last3oyears and wheretherefore large communities
 have not yet had time to develop. These two are the highest figures in the Province except in Peshawar,
 where the percentage is 47. The average for the other districts of these two groups is in each case 25^0 ;
 and the figures are then in regular sequence. The percentage of protected cultivation is larger in the
 2nd than in the ist and in the 3rd than in the 2nd group ; while the high rainfall of the 4th and 5th groups
 compensate for their scanty irrigation, and the large irrigation of the 3rd group is accompanied by a small
 rainfall.
       73. Figures for Indian Provinces compared.—Abstract No. 7 below gives the Panjab figures side
 by side with those for the other Indian Provinces. In Madras the village unit is largely artificial; as in
  Malabar, for instance, seven-eighths of the villages include more than 3,000 and one-half more than 5,000
  inhabitants, while one place of over 15,000 souls, 19 of over 10,000, and 313 of over 5,000 souls are classed
  in these tables as villages and not as towns, though I have shown them below as towns for the reason given
  in the foot-note to the abstract. The explanation is that the "village," or amsham as it is there called, has
  in very many parts of Madras the same meaning which, as I have explained in paragraph 66, attaches to
  it in some portions of the Panjab, being a purely artificial unit, and not really representing a conterminous
  group of houses. Excluding Madras the Panjab has, even if the Native States be included, the largest aver-
  age population per village and per village and town in the whole of British India, with the single exception of
   Bombay. Our large villages too are far more numerous throughout, with the same exception ; though the
   North-Western Provinces follow close upon us. In the matter of towns we are, in proportion to our popu-
   lation, somewhat in advance of the North-Western Provinces and far ahead of every other province.

 Para.;77--ll                                                         THE         DISTRIBUTION                                  OF THE P E O P L E
 Chap.ILi'
                                                         Part I.—Distribution over Towns and Villages.

       It will be noticed that the Buddhists live wholly in villages. They are, with the exception of a few
  Ladakhi coolies in Simla, confined to the Tibetan valleys of Lahul and Spiti. Next to them the Sikhs
 are most rural in their habits, not quite 3 percent. living in towns, while even that small proportion includes
  the numerous Sikh regiments of our Panjab cantonments. This follows naturally from the fact that the
  Sikhs are essentially agriculturists by occupation, 66 per cent, of them being Jats, and 20 per cent.
  more belonging to the castes which furnish village menials. The Musalmans come next, with 88-3 per
 cent, of rural population ; while the corresponding proportion for Hindus is only 85 per cent. This again
 is but natural, as the great mass of the commercial classes which are so largely represented in cities
 bel6n°-, in almost every district'in the Panjab, however great the general preponderance of Musalmans,
 to the&Hindu religion. Moreover the Musalmans preponderate to the west and the Hindus to the east of
 the Province; and,1 as has just been shown, the western population is far more rural than the eastern.
 Of the Jains more than half live in towns; and this again is due to the fact that this religion is almost
 confined to the mercantile community, and very largely to its more wealthy portion which is to be found in
 cities only. It is indeed surprising that in the Dehii and Hissar divisions as many as half the Jains should
 live in the villages. In no other division does the proportion rise as high as one-third. Christians are
 naturally found almost wholly in towns.
       77. Tendency of strangers to collect in the Towns.—The figures showing the distribution by
 religion bring out very clearly a fact which might indeed have been predicted a priori; and that is, that
 wherever a religion is represented by comparatively small numbers in a tract, there its numbers are to be
 found among the urban rather than among the rural population; in other words, that strangers and immi-
 grants are to be found in towns rather than in villages.
      The figures given below in Abstract No. 10, in which the divisions are arranged in order of pre-
 valence of the Musalman religion, exhibit this tendency very clearly :—
 Abstract No- 10, comparing the prevalence of each Religion with its proportion of Rural Population,

  It stands 6th (column 10) among the Divisions in respect of the magnitude of thu rurai component of the total population. It stands*i-V (column Yil in respect of

        In this table are shown, side by side for each religion, the proportion of the total population which
  belong to that religion and the proportion of its followers which live in towns ; while in the second part
  of the table is given the order of magnitude of the figures in each column of the first part. A comparison
  of the serial Nos. (columns 10 to 18) will show that among Musalmans the first 4, the middle 2, and
  the last 4 divisions agree ; among Hindus the first 4, the middle 3 and the last 3 ; amono- Sikhs the
  first 5 and the last 5 ; among Jains the first 5 and the last 2 ; in each case the population of each religion
  being most rural in those divisions where that religion is most prevalent, and conversely. That the serial
  order does not agree more exactly is in almost every case due to the influence which the ^enerallv rural or
- urban nature of the total population shown in columns r and 10 has upon the rural figures, wlnle it does
  not affect the figures of the other column. The largely urban nature of the Musalman population in the east
  is doubtless partly due to the number of Mahomedans attracted to the neighbourhood of Delhi under the
  Musalman dynasties, and settled with grants of land or revenue from the Emperors in the laro-e towns. So
  the still larger proportion of dwellers in towns among the Hindus of the west is due, as already noted, to
  their chiefly belonging to the trading classes. The Sikhs in Peshawar and the Derajat are ver\ largely in
   our military service or Khatris engaged in commerce.
         78. Proportions of urban and rural population for each sex.—The proportion of urban population is
   on the whole smaller among females than among males ; and this is what we should naturally expect to find
   since men who leave their families at home and go off in search of employment or to take service elsewhere'
   commonly move from villages to towns and not from towns to villages. At the same time it will be seen
   from the figures of Abstract No. 8, that this rule holds true in 19 only out of the 32 districts and in 8 only
   out of the 10 divisions; while in the Native States, with the exception of the Hill States, the urban propor-
   tion is very slightly larger for females than for males. An examination of the figures show that
              (1) where the urban proportion for females is larger than that for males the excess is usually
                     very small; far smaller on the average than the excess where the proportion for males i's
                     the larg 2r of the t\ vo;
                    26
                                              THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE PEOPLE.                                                T Para. 78.
                                                                                                                             LChap. II.

                                        Part, I.—Distribution over Towns and Villages.

              (2) that the urban proportion for females is in excess in the whole of the Delhi and Hiss£r
                     divisions except Sirsa; and in Ludhiana, Gurdaspur, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Shahpur, Jhang
                     and Muzaffargarh, and very slightly in Hushyarpur ; the excess being greatest in Rohtak
                     Karnal, Gurgaon, Jhang, Gujra'nwdla, and Hissar ;
              (3) that the excess of the urban proportion for males over that for females is markedly
                     largest in the whole of the Peshawar and Derajat Divisions, in Rawalpindi and Jahlam
                     and in Amritsar, Lahore, and Fi'rozpur ; while it is smallest in AmbaMa, J£!andhar, Multa'n,
                     and Montgomery. The figures for the proportion of urban population to every 10 000
                     of total population in each division are as follow:—

     These facts suggest the following as at any rate some of the causes which operate to produce the
difference under discussion. In the east of the Panjab, as in the Dehli and Hissax divisions, the more
wealthy and influential Mahomedans, who are likely to have several wives and many slave-girls and concu-
bines, are for the most part residents of the cities. In the trans-Jahlam portion of the Province on the other
hand, where the excess of the male proportion is markedly largest, this class is composed of chiefs of
tribes and rural notables who live almost wholly in the villages. Moreover the pardah feelingis far stronger
to the west than to the east of the Jahlam, so that men temporarily settling in towns would be more likely
to leave their women in the comparative privacy of their village. In Peshawar this is the almost uni-
versal custom. Again men marry at a much later age in the west than in the east of the Panjab, so that
young men going to towns in search of employment are more likely to have no families to take with them
in the former than in the latter. The large transport camps formed on the road to Peshawar in
connection with the operations in Kabul collected an unusual number of labourers in the towns of the
Peshawar and Rawalpindi divisions ; while the distress which unfavourable seasons had produced across our
upper frontier brought large numbers of the hill-men into our towns in search of employment. Again, the
excess of the female proportion is often greatest where the total population is most urban in its character
and the average village largest; in other words, where the town population includes the inhabitants of
places which are really villages in everything but size or the possession of municipal institutions.
Finally, in the recruiting districts the proportion of females in villages has a natural tendency to be
high, while the existence of large cantonments tends to raise the proportion of males in the towns.
      An examination of Abstract No. 9 shows that in no case is the urban proportion for females in
excess of that for males among members of the Sikh religion, that among Jains it is almost always in excess,
and that in every case the excess is larger according as the religion in which it occurs is less prevalent
in any particular tract. These results seem to follow naturally, from the tendency of people quitting
their ordinary domicile from any cause to leave their families behind them, whether they ordinarily live
in the villages like Sikhs, or in the towns like Jains; and from the fact already noticed that strangers
and immigrants settle chiefly in the towns ; and so when found in the villages often have not their families
with them.

            T h e figures of this a b s t r a c t a r e of course wholly devoid of g e n e r a l statistical value, the district unit of
  a r e a b e i n g wholly artificial. But they a r e not without a d m i n i s t r a t i v e significance. T h e g e n e r a l theory of t h e
  distribution of district charges is, t h a t t h e e l e m e n t s of t h e population and a r e a combined should b e tolerably
  c o n s t a n t . I h a v e a d d e d a column (No, 12) s h o w i n g t h e serial o r d e r of the districts in r e s p e c t of area. N o w
  if t h e district which h a s a l a r g e r population than a n o t h e r had a l w a y s a smaller a r e a a n d vice versa, t h e
. sum of t h e figures given opposite each district in columns 12 and 13 would always be 33. If it is g r e a t e r
  the district is less i m p o r t a n t , if smaller m o r e i m p o r t a n t in r e s p e c t of a r e a and population than it should
  be. T h e t e s t is p u r e l y qualitative a n d not q u a n t i t a t i v e ; but it is of some little interest. It shows that
  Simla, K o h a t , R o h t a k , Sirsa, Ludhi^nah, and Dehli fall, in that order, m a r k e d l y short of the a v e r a g e s t a n d -
  a r d ; while K a n g r a , R a w a l p i n d i , Lahore, A m b a l a , Multan a n d D e r a h Ismail m a r k e d l y exceed it. In the
  r e m a i n i n g districts t h e discrepancy, if any, is insignificant.            T h e a b s t r a c t further shows t h a t though several
  of o u r districts a r e l a r g e r in a r e a t h a n some of o u r divisions, y e t e a c h division is m o r e populous than a n y
  d i s t r i c t ; a n d t h a t t h e central divisions contain t h e largest and t h e w e s t e r n a n d southern divisions the

       8l. Indian charges compared with European Kingdoms-—1 think we often fail to realise the enor-
 mous areas and populations over which Indian officials have control, for want of familiar standards with
 which to compare them. Columns 7, 8, and 9 of abstract No. 13 on page 32 show the area, population, and
 numbers per square mile for the principal European and Indian countries as percentages on the corresponding
 figures for the Province; while columns io, 11, and 12 show their order of magnitude in these respects.
 In point of size the Province stands eighth on the list, only Russia in Europe, the Austrian and German
 Empires, France, Bengal, Spain and Sweden surpassing it, It is slightly larger than Prussia, one-fifth as
 large again as the British Isles, Hungary or Norway, one-quarter as large again as Italy or Austria, two
 and a half times as large as Turkey in Europe or England and Wales, four times as large as Portugal,
 five times as large as Ireland or Scotland, five-and-a half times as large as Greece, ten times as large as
 Switzerland, Denmark, or the Netherlands, and more than twelve times as large as Belgium. The Lieu-
 tenant-Governor of the Panjab rules over a population which is two-sevenths that of the Russian and
 half that of the German Empire, two-thirds that of the Austrian Empire, of France, and of the British Isles,
  and within a quarter of that of Italy, a fifth of that of Prussia, and a tenth of that of England and Wales.
  It is larger than that of Austria, one-third as large again as that of Spain, half as large again as that of
  Hungary, four times that of Ireland or Belgium, five times that of Portugal or Sweden, six times that of
  Scotland, Turkey in Europe, or the Netherlands, eight times that of Switzerland, eleven times that of
  Denmark or Greece, and fourteen times that of Norway. The Commissioner of Multan controls a tract
  nearly twice the size of Belgium, half as large again as the Netherlands or Denmark, a third as large again
  as Switzerland, two-thirds the size of Scotland, and more than a third as large as England and Wales ;
  while the Commissioner of Amritsar has under him a population double that of Norway, half as large again
  as that of Greece or Denmark, larger than that of Switzerland, nearly as large as that of Scotland, three-
  quarters that of the Netherlands or of Turkey in Europe, and one-eighth of that of England and Wales.
        82. The Deputy Commissioner of a district is the actual working and responsible head of every
  department of the administration within his charge excepting large public works, and is supposed to make
  himself personally acquainted with its every hole and corner; yet the district of Derah Ismail Khan is more
  than one-third as big again as Saxony, more than four-fifths the size of Belgium, three-fifths as large
  as Switzerland, two-thirds as large as Denmark, and very nearly a sixth of the size of England and Wales
  put together. So the population over whom the Deputy Commissioner of Ambala exercises a sway des-
  potic beyond the experience of Western Europe is more than half that of Denmark, Greece, or Norway,
  more than a third that of Switzerland or Saxony, nearly a third that of Scotland, a quarter of that of Portu-
  gal or.the Netherlands, and more than a fifth of that of Bavaria, Ireland, or Belgium. Yet the united
  administrative staff of these two districts consists of twelve Magistrates and Judges and three police offi-
  cers, of whom only eight are Europeans. The Hissar division has an executive staff of seven European
   and six Native officers, and there is not a soldier within 100 miles of its head-quarters ; yet its area and
  population are half those of Switzerland and two-thirds those of Denmark. 1 do not think it would be
  possible to illustrate more forcibly the significance of "Pax Indo-Britannica,'" the orderly and peaceable
   disposition of the people over whom we rule, or the vital importance of that prestige which now-a-days is
  held by some in such small account.

of the Slates are smaller than any of our four largest divisions. The population of the Pan jib is 46
per cent, of that of the whole United States.
