                                                                                                                                               L Chap.' II.

                                                 Part III.—Distribution over Area.

      It is not to be expected that the Panjab should, in comparison with other' countries, be densely popu-
lated. The great mountain tracts to the north and the arid steppes of its Western Plains include large
areas which are not habitable by man; and with a largely agricultural population, only 35 per cent, of its
total area is cultivated and only 70 per cent, even nominally culturable. Less than 40 years ago the
greater portion of the Province was subject to a military government of a very inferior type, war and
violence were rife in the land, and in many parts the peasant tilled his field with a sword at his side and
the Collector demanded the revenue at the head of a regiment; while 20 years earlier much of our south-
eastern border was practically a desert. Accordingly we find that out of the 63 separate tracts mentioned
in the Abstract, the Panjah stands as low as 34th. Compared with the other large Indian Provinces, the
population is less dense than that of Bengal, the North-Western Provinces, Madras, or Bombay proper, but
more dense than that of Berar, Haidar^bdd, Bombay with Sindh, Central India, Assam, the Central Prov-
inces, Rajputclna, Sindh, or Burmah. Turning to European countries, we find that the density for the
Province as a whole is about the same as for Ireland and the Austrian Empire, is not much more than
one-third that of Belgium and England and Wales, one-half that of the British Isles, and two-thirds that
of Italy and the German Empire ; while that of our British Territory is almost the same as in France, Bavaria
and Switzerland, and very little below that of the Indian Empire as a whole. But portions of the Panjab
stand very high in the scale. The Amritsar division, which is half the size of Belgium, is more thickly
populated than that most populous of all European countries ; while the Ambala division has about the
same density as have England and Wales and Saxony, and the Dehli division is more thickly peopled than
the Netherlands, and far more so than the British Isles. On the other hand the population of BabaValpur
is more sparse than that of any other country in the list except Russia, Sweden, and Norway ; while the
Derajat and Multan divisions and the Hill States stand only just above them, in company with Spain,
Servia, Greece, and Turkey in Europe.
     84. The figures for districts will be found in column 4 of Abstract No. 14 below. I give below, for
purposes of comparison, the ten highest and ten lowest densities among the 51 counties of England and
Wales, showing opposite each how many of our 32 districts have a higher density. Mr. Hunter says,
" Fertile France has only 180 people to the square mile ; while in crowded England, wherever the density
"approaches 200 to the square mile, it ceases to be a rural population, and has to live by manufactures,
" mines, or city industries." Seventeen of our thirty-two districts and four of our* ten divisions exceed
this standard ; while in fifteen of the seventeen districts and in all the four divisions the rural population
alone has a density of more than 200 to the square mile, and in five districts of more than double
that figure:—

     85. Density of rural population.—In considering a Province as a whole, or even its divisions where
population is counted by millions, the presence of a few cities, even though they be great ones if
measured by a Panjab standard, does not materially disturb the relative densities of population. But
as soon as we begin to examine smaller units, such as the district or its sub-division the tahsil, the
inclusion of towns deprives the figures for density of all significance. The boundary of the adminis-
trative unit is wholly artificial; and when it includes a targe city, the density of the population within it
can be. varied at pleasure by expanding or contracting its limits. Thus the district of Dehli has a rural
population of 345 per square mile, but the inclusion of the towns raises the figure to 504, or by 46 per
cent. So again, of the two tahsils of Dehli and Sunpat the latter is, excluding the towns, the more
thickly populated, the figures for rural population per square mile being 323 and 383 respectively; but
if the towns are taken into account the densities become 732 and 411. In fact, though the density of
the total population is interesting as affording the. only means of comparison with other countries,
and as indicating, when taken within a sufficiently wide limit, the number of souls which a given area
sustains, yet it is the density of the rural population which has the greatest practical value for the
Indian administrator. The population of the large towns is a thing apart; it is concentrated in definite
points, and the cities themselves are recognised as separate administrative units. Thus what chiefly
concerns the district officer is, the manner in which the great mass of the population which inhabits
the villages and cultivates the fields are distributed over .the wide plains which yield them the means
of livelihood.

the densities of the rural population for the great Indian Provinces. The figures per square mile are as

      ' The decrease in density as we pass from the great Gangetic plains of Bengal and the North-Western
  Provinces across the central watershed of India to the Indus system of the Panjab is most remarkable,
  and it will be presently seen that this change does not suddenly occur on the border of our Province, but
  that the high density is carried across the Jamria and along the foot of the Himalayas, and only gradually
  diminishes as we approach the arid western plains and southern wastes, till in our south-western districts
  it falls almost as low as in the neighbouring deserts of Sindh.
        87. Conditions which determine density of population.—Abstract No. 14 on page 37 shows the
  density of rural and total population for our districts arranged in order of magnitude of the former figures,
  together with statistics regarding rainfall, cultivation, culturable area, and irrigation, which help to explain
  the variations in the figures.
        The village population of the Panjab consisting almost wholly of husbandmen, together with the
  priests, traders, and menials attached to them, the agricultural capacity of each district practically deter-
  mines the density of its rural population. Now for agriculture in India two things are necessary, cultu-
  rable soil, and a supply of water either natural or artificial. The culturable area obviously suggests
  itself as the factor of primary importance, and in a certain sense it is so, as it definitely limits the possibi-
  lity of agricultural development. But it is not of such capital importance as it would appear to be at first
  sight. Where a country is fully developed and agricultural expansion is approaching the limits
  within which physical conditions confine it, the tract with the largest proportion of culturable area will
  naturally have the densest population, other factors, such as the fertility of the culturable soil, being
  constant.     But the Panjab as a whole is by no means fully developed; as yet only one-half of
' its culturable area is under the plough ; and under these circumstances it is natural that the popu-
  lation should tend to collect in greatest numbers in those tracts where an ample water supply ren-
  ders the culturable area immediately available for cultivation. Unfortunately, also, the figures for cul-
  turable area given in column 7 of the Abstract are eminently calculated to mislead. It appears that the
  Settlement Department have returned as culturable all the great grazing grounds of the Western
  Plains. Now there is no doubt whatever that the soil so returned is intrinsically fertile, and capable, if
  water were forthcoming, of yielding a sufficient return to the husbandman. But there is equally little
  doubt that the scanty rainfall which prevails west of the meridian of Lahore renders the great mass of the
  tract for all practical purposes unculturable without artificial irrigation. Where such irrigation exists, and
  within the limits.to which it extends, cultivation is possible. Beyond these limits, save in riverain tracts
  or local hollows of very limited area, cultivation is impossible; while the great depth of the subsoil water
  renders irrigation from wells, in the present condition of Panjab agriculture, unprofitable, and the canals
  which can alone supply the necessary water are as yet non-existent.
       88. Thus the supply of water becomes the most important factor in the conditions which determine the
 density of rural population in the Panjab. It may be either natural or artificial ; and the natural tendency
 obviously is for population to first occupy those tracts, other conditions being equal, where an ample rain-
 fall enables them to dispense with those artificial aids the creation and employment of which involve con-
 siderable expenditure both of capital and labour. But these tracts once occupied, other considerations
 come into play as population increases and the standard of agricultural practice advances. The tracts in
 which the rainfall is heaviest are often not those in which the physical conformation of the ground and the
 nature of the soil are best adapted to the needs of the husbandman, while the most valuable crops can
 seldom be grown at all, and can never be cultivated to perfection, unless the rainfall be supplemented by
 artificial irrigation of some sort. Thus, given that the rainfall is fairly sufficient, those tracts in which a
 high spring level and a fertile soil render extensive irrigation from wells at once possible and profitable,
 tend to develop fastest and most highly and to attract the largest population in proportion to their area.
       The action of Government in constructing those great canals which bring water to so large a portion of
 our thirsty land has also introduced another element into the question ; for the use of canal water is of all
 methods of irrigation that which demands least labour from the cultivator, and, at least at the first,
 yields him the most abundant out-turn.
       89. From the above considerations we arrive at the following cardinal conditions as primarily deter-
 mining the density of the rura>population in the Panjab—•
             (1) That where the proportion of the culturable to the total area is actually small, a dense popu-
                     lation is impossible;
             (2) That where the rainfall is scanty, the population, in the absence of canal irrigation, will be
                     scanty also ;
             (3) That, given a fairly sufficient rainfall, the population will be densest where circumstances have
                     permitted or encouraged the development of extensive irrigation from wells or canals.
        I will now examine the figures of Abstract No. 14 in the light of the above axioms. It is not to be
  expected that they will fall into an exact sequence, such as might have been predicted by the application
  of our formulae. There are many conditions of minor importance which carry more or less weight in differ-
  ent parts of the Province. The intrinsic fertility of the alluvial soil of our plains, wonderfully uniform as it
  is on the whole considering the vastness of the area with which we are dealing, does vary sufficiently to
  afEect seriously the capacity of certain tracts to support an agricultural population. The physical conforma-
  tion of the country, while it in some places renders a dense population impossible, often affords pasture
  to extensive flocks and herds which supplement the produce of the fields ; and the means of cheap and ready
  carriage afforded by the existence of a railway, by raising prices and increasing the profits of agriculture,
  have no inconsiderable effect in attracting population. Moreover our figures only represent in the most
  general manner the actual circumstances of each district; for physical conditions vary widely within its
  boundaries, our information is often imperfect, and our standards not always uniform. But it will be found
  that the considerations which I have indicated above determine the general distribution of the rural
• population, and that is all that can be expected without a discussion in greater detail than either my
 .space or my information will admit of. I shall assume that the physical characteristics of the several tracts

      90. District figures examined.—The districts in which the conditions of sufficient rainfall, nearness of
spring level, and a fertile soil are combined in the highest degree, are the eight districts which run along the
foot of the hills from the Jamna to the Jahlam, and form my submontane zone and the northern tract of the
Eastern Plains, These eight districts stand among the first nine in our list. I exclude Simla altogether, as
being utterly abnormal. Next to them in respect of the specified conditions come the four districts which
lie in the Jamna zone; and these four, with the eight just mentioned, complete the first twelve districts of the
Abstract. Immediately after them in order of density follow the three districts of Lahore, Firozpur,
and Gujranwala, the first two of which are included in the central block of the Eastern Plains, the
next most fertile and best watered of the tracts into which I divided the Province, while Gujranwala was
only excluded from it because it lay west of the meridian which I took as my boundary (see footnote to
Section 19). These 15 districts stand among the 21 districts which have the largest rainfall in the Province.
The remaining 6 districts arranged in order of density are Rawalpindi with only 39 per cent,, Jahlam
with 42 per cent., Hazara with 31 per cent., Hissar, Kangra with only 15 per cent., and Kohcit with 16
per cent, of its area culturable; ot which all, with the exception of Hissar, are hill districts and contain large
mountain areas, which where not absolutely uninhabitable, are at least incapable of cultivation. The

first three stand 17th, 18th, 19th on the list 1 , and following immediately after the fifteen districts already
discussed. The last two stand 25th and 30th, their small culturable area neutralising their ample rainfall
and putting them almost at the bottom of the list, though a considerable pastoral population raises Kangra,
and the fact that it lies on a still unsettled border depresses Kohat. Hissar is 20th in order of rainfall,
and much of it was not very long ago wholly uninhabited.
      At the bottom of the list come the seven districts of the Western Plains and the two districts of the
southern zone of the Eastern Plains with the scantiest rainfall in the Province, and Bannu with a small
rainfall as well as a small culturable area. These ten districts stand among the twelve lowest in the list,
Kangra and Kohat, which have been discussed above, making up the number. They also stand among
the twelve districts of the Province which have the smallest rainfall, the other two being Lahore and
Peshawar which stand 15th and 16th on the list, and in which the irrigation from the Bari Doab Canal
and from hill streams reduces the proportion of unirrigated cultivation. Between these two groups come
the frontier district of Peshawar, and the districts of Rawalpindi, Jahlam, and Hazara which have been
already noticed. This completes the tale of districts for the Province.
      pi. Descending to greater detail, the five districts which stand highest of the eight first mentioned above
are Jalandhar, Sialkot, Amritsar, Gurdaspur, and Ludhianah, or precisely those i\ve in which the presence
of a canal and a railway, and a distance from the hills sufficient to ensure the absence of broken ground
or of boulder subsoil in which wells are impossible, but not so great as to reduce the rainfall too largely,
permit agriculture to reach the highest level of excellence which it attains in the Panjab. In the matter
of rainfall all but one of these first eight districts stand above the next seven, which complete the first
group of fifteen ; while of these latter seven the four of densest population are also the four of largest
rainfall, with the single exception of Rohtak where a canal assists with its water the finest Jat communities
in the Province. The last ten districts stand almost in order of rainfall, the only exceptions of any moment
being Muzaffargarh and Multan where inundation canals partly compensate for the niggardliness of the
seasons, and Sirsa which is lower than its rainfall would place it, as it was-an uninhabited waste only some
sixty years ago.
      Of the thirty-one districts under discussion only seven have less than two-thirds of their total area
returned as culturable. Of these Hoshyarpur, with 63 per cent, of culturable, stands 6th on the list ; but its
position at the foot of the Himalayan range more than compensates for the presence of unculturabie hills.
Rawalpindi, Jahlam and Hazara, with from 30 to 40 per cent, of culturable, occupy the centre of the list,
their small culturable area and their abundant rainfall operating in opposite directions to give them an
intermediate density of population. Bannu, with 54 per cent, of culturable soil, stands 26th, but this is
chiefly due to its small rainfall; while Kangra and Kohat, which are the only two districts with more than
three-quarters of their area unculturabie, stand at the bottom of the list and have already been discussed.

bala where Pipli has 244 and Rupar 520 per square mile, in Bannu where the density of Lakki is 56 and of
Bannu tahsil 221, and in Rawalpindi where Pindigheb has 60 and Gujar Khan 236 to the square mile.

 Chap. II. J

                                                          Part IV.—Distribution among Houses and Families.



                                          PART IV.-DISTRIBUTION AMONG HOUSES AND FAMILIES.

       97. Significance of house Statistics.—I have already briefly indicated in paragraphs 30, 31 the difficul-
  ties which were encountered in deciding what should be considered a " house " for Census purposes; and the
  subject is discussed at length in the chapter on Preliminary Operations in Book II of this Report. In that
• chapter, which I wrote before examining the figures, I stated that I believed the " house " as recorded in the
  present Census to be comparatively valueless for statistical purposes ; and the figures themselves only confirm
  that opinion. I have already described in the passages above quoted the common courtyard, opening by a
  single doorway from the street, round which are ranged the buildings occupied by families closely connected
  with one another, and by their cattle. It was intended that in the villages at least the " h o u s e " should
 -correspond with the courtyard wherever it was found to exist and was not of unmanageable size. And
1
  many of the Deputy Commissioners expressly state that this was the course generally adopted, though some
  few add that they considered it a wrong one, and substituted for it the numbering of individual buildings wher-
  ever they had the opportunity of doing so. Yet the figures scarcely seem, judging from my own limited experi-
  ence of the Province, to bear out this statement, I can hardly believe that in the villages of the Dehli district
  there are on an average less than two, in Karndl only i£, and in Rohtak only 1^ families living in each
  courtyard. I suspect the fact is that the permission to sub-divide where the enclosure was large was freely
  taken advantage of, and that the " h o u s e " which was numbered was often merely that unit which seemed
  in each case most convenient for the practical purposes of enumeration. Still in a very large majority of
  cases that unit would correspond with the courtyard. On former occasions the " enclosure " and " house,"
  corresponding respectively with our "house " and " family," were numbered separately. But the result does
  not seem to have been successful. In 1855 the average number of souls per enclosure was 0/99, but the
  figures fluctuate in the most extraordinary manner between the two extremes of 20/90 and 5*97. In 1868
  the average was 7'62, and the fluctuations hardly less remarkable between 23*38 and 5'16. In the present
  Census the average for British Territory was 6*96, the figures ranging from 9*73 to 4'gy.
       98. Our results at any rate disclose none of those startling aberrations which appear in the figures of
 the two former Censuses ; and, while I do not think they can be accepted as accurately representing the
 statistics for any single form of building or enclosure, which indeed they were not supposed to do
 under the strict letter of the instructions, I do think that in the villages at least, where the difficulties
 were less and the numbers dealt with are enormous, and in the totals where the numbers are still larger, they
 may be taken as representing with a very fair degree of accuracy the distribution of the people among
 houses or small enclosures ; while the relative results probably express almost exactly the relative degrees
 in which the population of various portions of the Province is collected into common courtyards or
 dispersed over isolated houses. In the towns the difficulties, as explained elsewhere, were so great that
 uniformity was almost impossible, the numbers dealt with were generally too small for individual pecu-
 liarities of structure or treatment to neutralise one another, and the figures of column 12 in Table XX,
 Appendix A present variations which are in all probability often due to diversity of system rather than
 to dissimilarity in the actually existing conditions.
      99- Figures discussed.—Abstract No. 17 shows the number of families and of persons per house in vil-
 lages and towns respectively for the districts and major states of the Province. The former I consider the
 more valuable of the two sets of statistics. The number of persons per family, to be discussed presently,
 shows us the size of the groups into which the people are associated round a common hearth. The number of
 families per house shows how far those groups are collected within a common building or enclosure. The
 number of souls per house is merely an arithmetical deduction from these two data. If indeed the
 house were a single building, as in England, the figures would afford some indication of the amount of
 house-room enjoyed by the people ; though even then the inclusion of the single-roomed hut and the town-
 house of several flats in the same set of figures would greatly reduce their significance. But the courtyard
 is so indefinite a unit and capable of so great expansion, that the number of persons living in each tells
 us little of the closeness with which they are packed.

are riot based upon uniform data, and much stress cannot be laid on the comparison ; but the tendency is
in accord with the general progress (if it is progress) towards severalty, which every day becomes more
and more marked under our occidental rule.
      101. It will be noticed that the number of families per house is far more uniform in the town than in
the village, being larger for towns than for villages where the average for villages is low, and larger for
villages than for towns where the average for villages is high. This is only a natural consequence of the
greater uniformity of the conditions within-urban limits, and of the abandonment of caste restrictions
which poverty and want of space impose upon the poorer portion of our town population.
     102. Unoccupied houses.—The question of unoccupied houses is discussed in the chapter on Prelimi-
nary Operations in Book II of the Report. In the whole Province there are 28, and in British Territory
27 unoccupied for every 100 occupied houses in villages only; but the proportion rises as high as 68 in
Muzaffargarh, 59 in Rohtak, 46 in Bah&walpur, 44 in Jalandhar, and 41 in Gurgaon. On the other hand,
it falls as low as 17 in Firozpur and Derah Ismail, 15 in Nabha, 14 in Pesha\var, 13 in Hazara, 11 in
Jahlam, 10 in Sirsa and Chamba, and below 10 in several of the larger Hill States. The village figures for
divisions are as follow :—
          Delhi                                           37           Amritsar        .   .    .       .   .   .   .   27
          Hiss&-                                          35           Luhott                                           2

          Mnlt&i .    .   .       •    •     •    • - -   35           Derajat .

          Jalandhar                                                    Peshawar
Generally it may be said that the proportion of unoccupied houses is largest where the two extremes of
density or sparseness of population, and of high careful cultivation or large areas under inferior crops
prevail, and lowest where intermediate conditions obtain and in the hills. But there are striking exceptions
for which no explanation but diversity of system can be offered. In Gurgaon, I fear, the high figure tells
a tale of death and emigration due to disease and distress. In the villages the greater part of these unoccu-
pied houses consist either of huts built out in the fields for the shelter of the husbandman, or of buildings
within the courtyard and occupied by the cattle. The former are classed as houses, because the rule that
watchers in the field should be enumerated as if at home was not properly understood while the house-num-
berino" was going on ; the latter, because one or more members of the family generally sleep with the cattle for
security against theft, and also because in many cases the dwellings occupied by people and cattle are
identical in structure, and the latter are always liable to be turned out to make room for a visitor or to
suit the family convenience. The inclusion of the former class of buildings among the unoccupied
houses seems to explain the general rule stated above which governs the figures. Where a dense
population is collected in great villages and cultivates the superior crops, the fields need more constant
attention and are better worth protecting; while where the area under the plough is large in proportion
to population, and scattered throughout the jungle wherever a local hollow collects the surface drainage,
the crops must be watched by night if anything is to be saved from the havoc caused by wild animals.
In both extremes outlying huts are more common than under intermediate conditions. In the hills and in
the Peshawar and Rawalpindi divisions, where the cold of a winter night is not to be trifled with, these
huts are occupied in the summer only.
     103. In towns the proportion of unoccupied to every 100 occupied houses is invariably much larger
than in villages, averaging 47 for British Territory and the Province. It is also far more uniform, though it
also ranges between 92 in Derah Ghizi and 20 in Koh^t. The bulk of these unoccupied houses in the towns
consist of shops, mosques, and other similar buildings only occupied by day. In the villages the
shop-keeper almost invariably has his shop and house in the same building. In the towns the wealthier
traders live away from their places of business ; and, as Mr. Drummond remarks, "the separation of the
shop and the dwelling house is an asra in the history of every progressive tradimg family." Still among
the shop-keepers of moderate means one of the family often sleeps in the shop to save the expense of a
private watchman ; and where, as is not unfrequently the case, he also cooks his meals in the shop, it
should be, and probably was, returned as an occupied house. It may be that the increase at successive
enumerations of the proportion of unoccupied to occupied houses in individual towns may vary with the
commercial prosperity of the town. On the present occasion we have no earlier figures with which to make
comparison. Mr.' Drummond suggests that in new towns it seems more the fashion than it was in old ones
to build the dwelling-house in connection with the shop. I cannot say either from my own experience
or from that of others how generally true this statement may be.
     104. The confocal family.—The " family" or group which eats food cooked at a common hearth is the
unit which of all other social units is most familiar to the native mind, and the statistics which relate.
to it are probably among the most accurate which we have obtained. It is true that, owing to my own
negligence as explained in paragraph 55, there may have been some confusion about the treatment of
travellers and the like ; but at the most the population in question is, in the villages at least, so infinitesimally
small that the figures, will not have been appreciably affected. Abstract No. 18 on page 45 gives the
number of souls per family in villages and towns respectively for the districts and major states of the Province,
      The first point which strikes us on glancing at the figures is the utter absence of those larg*e undivided
families which the student is so accustomed to associate with the very idea of Hindu society. In Kangrag5,
and in Rohtak 89 per cent, of the village population are Hindus, yet the average family consists of 4"$7 souls
in theone and of 475 in the other. In Eastern Bengal indeed, the great undivided family, living and having
all things in common, and cultivating under the guidance of a single head the land which is jointly owned
by the whole family, occasionally comprises "in Calcutta, and possibly even in the rural tracts, as many as
" 300 or 400 individuals including servants ; while it is probably usual for a family to amount to something
 "between 50 and ioo 1 ;" but such an institution is absolutely unknown inthePanjAb. Mr. Drummond remarks
                              1
                                  Calcutta Review, Vol. L X I X , I874, p. 207, quoted by Mr. Tupper.

that to the Panjab peasant ;the tribe or the village community supplies the place of the undivided
family: "the young men of the village are his brothers and the grey beards his fathers, the children
"following the village herd as he drives the cattle to their rest in the common pen his nephews and nieces,
" the field is his home, and the settlement his undivided family." It would require a far closer knowledge
than I possess of the constitution of village society in Bengal to decide how far the parallel holds good.
But the remark, like most of Mr. Drummond's .remarks, is eminently suggestive ; and it is not impossible that
it contains the germ of an idea which, fully worked out, would explain the utter unsuitability to the condi-
tions under which society exists in the Panjab, of that compilation of Bengal1 custom, overlaid by the glosses
of generations of Bengali commentators and interpreted by Bengali Pandits, which under the misleading
title of Hindu law our Courts have endeavoured to impose upon the country at large. This much at least
is certain, that the distinction in matters of inheritance between the joint and the divided family upon
which so much stress is laid by the Hindu law of the Pandits, is unknown at any rate to the peasantry
of the Panjdb ; and that if it obtains anywhere, it is among the Brahmans and mercantile and writer
classes of the cities, who in this as in many other respects affect a purism in religious and other matters
treated of in the Shdstras which is quite foreign to the more primitive customs of their rustic brethren.
     105. The usual course of affairs in a Panjlb household is somewhat as follows. The children grow up
and marry as a matter of course under their father's roof. After a time the girls go off to their husbands,
and the sons bring their wives home to live with them ; but the latter are still mere youths, and the family
continues to live together. As however the sons and daughters-in-law grow up, and as new brides are
brought to the family hearth, dissensions arise among the women which at last become unbearable, and
the elder sons with their wives and children separate, each family receiving a part of the common house or
a separate building in the common courtyard, and cooking its meals and managing its income and domestic
expenses separately. After a while the parents grow old and are received into one of the younger groups,
or live with all by turns. So matters go on till after some generations the group of families becomes too
large for the house or courtyard ; another is built, and a further separation takes place, the more closely-
related families living together in either of the two buildings. Sometimes the separation of the sons is
deferred till the death of the father dissolves the common tie; but It is more usual for it to take place as
soon as they have married and grown up.
      106. The proprietary group.—But this separation of confocal families is a purely domestic
arrangement, and extends only to expenditure on food, clothes, and the like. It results almost invariably
from disagreements among the women, and does not as a rule affect the land, in the management of which
they have no voice. The large undivided family, if it is unknown as a social or domestic unit, still forms
to a great extent the basis of property in the land of the Panjab. On our western frontier, where tribal
organisation is strongest and tribal tenures prevail, the land is most commonly held jointly by the
tribe or clan, the shares in a single village sometimes numbering as many as 36,000. But I would go
further than this. I would say that, even where the village community has most completely superseded
the tribe as the owner of land, thejoint family was till not very long ago, and as far as landed rights only
are concerned, almost co-extensive with the proprietary body of that community, or at least of each of its
sections. I believe that I am only exaggerating the truth when I say that the bhayachara village, where
land is held in severalty, is an invention of our own. I have given at length, in Chapter VII of my Settle-
ment Report of Karni.1, my reasons for thinking that such was the case in that district ; and though the
Sikh revenue system, under which strangers were freely admitted to cultivating rights which could hardly
be distinguished from ownership since ownership itself gave little more than the right to cultivate, doubt-
less obscured the original constitution of the village, yet the more I study the settlement reports of the
 Panjab proper, the more I am convinced that what I found to have existed in old days in the Karnal dis-
trict was the rule in the Panjab, at least wherever the village community was fully developed, to a much
wider extent than is generally admitted. In the report already alluded to I wrote as follows:—
            " I t h i n k t h e r e a m be but little doubt t h a t , till the English rule, individual property in land, in the sense in which we undcr-
" stand it, was unknown in the tract. Each village held the area surrounding its homestead, the dividing boundaries being scarcely
" defined. Land was plentiful, cultivators were scarce, almost any body was welcome to break up as much a^ be could cultivate, and
" t h e owner who induced a t e n a n t to settle and bear a share of the burden of the revenue conferred a benefit upon the c o m m u n i t v
" a t large.             *         *    * * The ancestral shares of each household of the land-owning c o m m u n i t y were carefully preserved, a n d
" regulated the interest of each in the waste lands a n d the a d j u s t m e n t of village j o i n t income and expenditure ; b u t the area of land
"-held by each in c u ' t i v a t i n g possession varied with its ability to cultivate rather t h a n with its rateable share in the village. The
" theory, however, t h a t the plot of land so held by the members of a family was their own to do w h a t they pleased with, was wholly
" f o r e i g n to tlie ideas of the people. Sales of land were unknown ; and when the owner b e r i m e , frcni failure of appliances, unable to
" c u l t i v a t e as much as formerly, the community arranged if possible for the cultivation of the abandoned fields, while the owner
" remained, responsible for t h e revenue of only so much land as he actually held. When we first made a record of rights in land,
 " o u r primary object was to obtain a record of liability for revenue, which depended wholly upon c u l t i v a t i n g possession. S u t we
" went further than t h i s . W e of course preserved as a rule, though n o t always witli entiie success, the distinction between owner
" and t e n a n t ; b u t instead of recording each constituent household of the proprietary body as entitled t o a fractional share in the
" village, and as merely holding in cultivating possession the land cultivated by its members or by tenants whom they had settled,
" we recorded and treated it, or rather the individual who was its temporary head, as absolute owner of t h a t land, and entered as
 " common property only such land as was either uncultivated, or was held by tenants who had been settled by the village in general
 " o r by one of its sub-divisions. The proprietary rights so created are now, of course,.indefeasible. But 1 believe such property in
 " s e v e r a l t y , Eased solely upon actual possession, t o have been entirely a creation of our own ; t h a t before our time the breaking up
" of land gave the cultivator a r i g h t to hold t h a t land undisturbed so long as he paid the revenue on it, b u t gave him no further
 " l'igtits; and t h a t i t gave him t h i s much w h e t h e r he was an owner or n o t . "
     By "village community" I here mean a natural group of families having common interests in land.
Where, as described in sections 65, 66, the village is purely artificial, the real community, the real pro-
prietary unit is limited to the individual hamlet or well, and does not comprise all the separate hamlets or
wells which we may happen to have included within a common boundary.

      107. But whether the correctness of the above description of the old land-tenure is or is not admitted
to be applicable to the village community as a whole, it is certain that it exactly describes the manner in
which land is commonly held in joint property by groups of closely-related owners which are very much
larger than the confocal " family" to which our figures relate. The sons wrhen they separate their domestic
concerns at the instigation of their wives, seldom separate their interests in the family land ; and it is no
uncommon thing to rind the descendants of a common ancestor of several generations back holding the
 estate in joint ownership which is strictly regulated by ancestral shares. The actual cultivation of the
land is however, from considerations of convenience, very commonly in the hands of much smaller groups ;
and here the size of the holdings is regulated rather by the appliances of cultivation in the possession
of each group than by their rights of property in the land. Where there are seven or eight stalwart
brothers or cousins with a corresponding number of oxen they will hold a large area, while the widow
with a family of young children will cultivate a small plot through a tenant. When however the stalwart
brothers die childless and the widow's sons grow up to manhood, a redivision of the land will be made ;
for some sort of periodical redistribution, whether regulated by custom or voluntarily made as occasion
arises, follows almost as a matter of necessity wherever ancestral shares regulate proprietary right. As the
 group of joint owners expands, and increasing distance from the common ancestor relaxes the ties of
 kinship, actual separation of rights at length takes place, though not as a rule between individuals so
 much as between groups of families, and the cycle recommences.
      108. The cultivating association.—There is another institution, connected with the cultivation ol
rather than with property in the land, which appears to me to take the place in the Panjib of that house-
community, common among Slav races, which has so often been described by writers on primitive institu-
tions, and which differs from the joint family in that it is based in part upon common property in land and
not wholly upon common descent, and recognises separate property in cattle and movables, and from the
association that I am about to describe in that its members share a common house and table. In the Dehli
Territory the institution to which I refer is called the lu.7ia) and it obtains, I believe, in some form or other
almost throughout the Province. It consists of an association for the purposes of agriculture, and exists in
two typical forms the actual conditions of which I proceed to describe, connecting them by a train of suppo-
sititious circumstances which I believe to explain the transition from the one to the other. When, in an
undeveloped tract where land is plentiful and labour scarce, a group of owners find themselves in possession
of far more land than can be cultivated by their own resources, they call in to their aid a number of out-
siders, commonly landless menials or men of inferior castes, who become partners in the cultivation. The
work is done by all jointly, a share of the produce is set aside as representing the proprietary right and
is divided among the owners of the land, and the remainder is distributed over the oxen and men actually
employed in the cultivation. If the owners are Rajputs, who have a hereditary disinclination for manual
labour of any sort and a special contempt for the actual operation of ploughing, which they consider derog-
atory, they find most of the oxen and little of the labour, and an ox takes twice the share of a man ] . If
the owners are Jats, who are husbandmen from the womb, the ox and the man will share equally.
      Time goes on, the community expands, the land remains the same, agriculture develops, and the pro-
prietary group finds that it can furnish enough hands for the cultivation of its fields without the aid of
others. It cultivates jointly as before ; but in the distribution of the produce no regard is paid to the area
of land owned or held by each family, and the division is based solely upon the number of ploughs which
have been contributed, that is to say, upon the share of the labour which has been undertaken by each.
One family may own a share representing 40 acres and contribute but one plough, while another which
owns 10 acres only contributes four ploughs. The five ploughs cultivate the 50 acres, and the latter family
takes four times as large a share of the whole produce as does the former. Where a family finds itself un-
able to furnish the whole number of hands required to make up the number of ploughs tor which its oxen
suffice, it associates with itself an outsider on much the same terms as obtain in the first tvpe just described ;
but here the outsider has to deal, not with the association as a whole, but only with the individual family.
      I have spoken of the second type of association as existing within the group of closely related fami-
lies, and I have little doubt that such was its primitive form ; in fact the disregard paid to rights of
property in distributing the produce of the land almost proves that the institution had its origin among
families or households which held the land jointly, and whose interests in the produce were therefore
regulated by the shares they bore in the cultivation. It is in this respect precisely analogous to the custom.
so common in the Panjab, of distributing the burden of the land revenue over ploughs without regard in
proprietary shares. But, at any rate in that part of the Province which has been longest under our rule.
and in which separation of interests and the substitution of contract for custom have accordingly made the
greatest advance, the association is in its present form voluntary, is made for one year only, and is not
necessarily confined to any group of closely related households ; though in actual practice it often subsists
for years, and between families which are near of kin 2 .
      109. The joint Family, the House-community, and the Village-community. —Thus, though the Pan-
jab community divides itself on social grounds into small groups distinguished one from another by tht-
separation of hearth and board, yet the large undivided family still forms the unit of proprietary rio-hts
in land; and this was probably very much more markedly the case before our settlement record of rights
confused separate cultivating possession with property in severalty. And even where the land is h'elcl
 in separate ownership, associations of families or individuals for the purpose of cultivation take the place nf'
the house-communities of more primitive races.

     One of the most striking points about the figures is their extraordinary uniformity. The two extremes
reached among the 32 districts of British Panjab are 5-69 and 3-38 ; while 28 of the 32 lie between 5-15
and 4'19, the deviation being less than 19 per cent. The differences are so small that they may almost be?
said to be accidental, and any detailed examination would be unprofitable. But one fact may be mentioned
which probably accounts for the position at the head of the list which the Hill States occupy. It is that
throughout the Panjab hills be gar or forced labour is exacted, not by headsbutby hearths; so that so long
as brothers remain joint, they have to do collectively only as much begar as each of them would have to
do if they separated. The result is, in Mr. Anderson's opinion, not so much that separation is prevented,
as that it is concealed.
     111. The Tibetan Family in Spiti.—The lowest figure reached would appear to be in Spiti, where the
average is only 3-3 persons per family. The form which family life assumes in these wild Tibetan vallevs
is so peculiar that I make no apology for extracting the following description from Mr. Alex. Anderson's
Census Report:—

          " 1'ang chungpa, or occupant of even a smaller house, t h a t is the g r a n d f a t h e r . "

      112. The Family in towns.—It will be noticed that the average family is smaller in towns than in
 villages in all but three districts, and that in many cases the difference is very considerable. This was
 only to be expected. Among the richer classes, indeed, a plurality of wives, concubines, and servants pro-
 bably swell the town family to much larger dimensions than are reached in the villages. But this excess
 is more than counterbalanced by the number of men of the poorer classes who flock to the large towns
 in search of employment, leaving their families in the villages.
       113. Tendency towards severalty.—The average number of souls per family in the three several
 enumerations of the Panja'b population is as follows:—1855, 4'53 ; 1S68, 4-27; 1881,4*56. This would
 seem to show that the tendency of the family had been, if anything, to increase in size. But I am not
.certain what was meant in 1868 by a " house," which corresponded with our " family," as their " enclosure"
 did with our "house." The circular instructions then issued defined a " house or family as those who live
 together and ordinarily cook their food-at the same hearth;" and this is precisely the " family" of the pres-
 ent Census. But the same instructions direct that each house shall be numbered " by a rough ticket or by
 paint on the entrance ;" and the writer of the Census Report dwells upon the distinction between masonry
 and mud "houses," and points out that the smaller number of souls in the average house implies '' increas-
 ed house accommodation, a sure indication of prosperity." There would thus appear to have been some
 confusion between the structural and the social units ; and though the number of occupied buildings should

         115. T h e P a n j a b d u r i n g t h e 18th c e n t u r y . — T h e first half of the 18th c e n t u r y was one of unusual
turmoil even for I n d i a ; and as has ever been the case when fighting is going on, the P a n j a b was
in the very heart of the fray. As the century opened, the Sikhs, rapidly g r o w i n g into i m p o r t a n c e as
a military organisation, but as y e t possessed of no national spirit to restrain their excesses, thirsting
for r e v e n g e for the p e r s e c u t i o n s of the bigoted A u r a n g z e b a n d for the m u r d e r of the helpless family of their
a r e a t Guru Govind, and p r o m p t to profit by the dissensions which followed on the death of Bahadur Shah,
r a v a g e d t h e whole eastern portion of the Province from the J a m n a to the S a t l u j , a n d laid the n o r t h e r n a n d
central tracts under contribution. T h e invasion of the g r e a t P e r s i a n freebooter Nadir Shah followed close
upon their punishment, a n d swept like a w a v e of death through the Panjab, r a v a g i n g and d e s t r o y i n g all
that lay in its course. A n d the first half of the century was fitly closed by the famines of 1753 and 1759.
         116. T h e latter half of the s a m e c e n t u r y witnessed o n e continuous struggle b e t w e e n the M a h r a t t a s
in the east, the Durranis in the west, a n d the Sikhs in the c e n t r e , for t h e possession of the P a n j a b
plains, varied only by the rise a n d fall of petty m a r a u d i n g chiefs of every country u n d e r an Indian
heaven, Rajputs, Mughals, Jats, Biloches, P a t h a n s , even F r e n c h m e n and Englishmen, who saw in the
d e c a y of the Mughal empire and the universal a n a r c h y which prevailed, an opportunity to rise to power
a n d to a m a s s wealth by war and r a p i n e . E i g h t times within twice as many y e a r s did A h m a d Shah invade
t h e P a n j a b ; eight times had he to fight his way through the Sikh armies which s p r a n g up on his path
like Jason's foes; eight times was his d e p a r t u r e from the Province the signal for the Sikhs and M a h r a t t a s to
fly at each other's throats ; until even he g a v e up the struggle in despair, and left the Sikh m/s/s to e x t e n d
their c o n q u e s t s , always b y hard fighting, till they w e r e masters of the whole of the P a n j a b from the J a m n a
to the Indus a n d from K a n g r a a n d J a m m u to Hansi a n d Multan, a n d , h a v i n g won them, to quarrel over
their possessions. T h e desolation which A h m a d S h a h ' s a r m y carried in its route is expressed by the
s a y i n g still current a m o n g the wild tribes of M o n t g o m e r y : " W h a t one eats and drinks is one's own ; the rest
is A h m a d S h a h ' s . " During the intervals b e t w e e n his incursions the M a h r a t t a s overran the country and
took Multan and Lahore, a n d w e r e presently followed by the Bhangi S i k h s —
"whose raids and cruelty live to this day in the memory of the peasants of MuzafEargarh." Meanwhile, " various men o£ in-
" fluence made themselves independent, and exercised all the privileges of independent rulers as regards fighting with each other, and
" robbing and murdering those weaker than themselves. Might was the only test of right, and in the absence of any general control-
" ling authority the country became a pre}' to the ambition of rival chiefs struggling for supremacy."
          It is impossible to open a history .of a n y part of the P a n j a b during these terrible fifty years, without
finding every p a g e occupied by one continuous story of war a n d bloodshed. T h e whole Province was
in a r m s . Almost every considerable village or small town had its local chief, with a band of followers
ready to fight for plunder or p o w e r ; and the i n c e s s a n t turmoil in which t h e s e g e n t r y kept the c o u n t r y was
i n t e r r u p t e d only when t h e y united a g a i n s t a common e n e m y from without.
      117. In t h e midst of all this misery came the " g r e a t famine," as the people still call it, of r 7 8 3 .
      In the east of the Panjab " the country was depopulated, the peasants abandoning their villages and dying in thousands of
"disease and want; the country swarmed with bands of thieves and highway robbers, and the state of anarchy was almost incon-
" ceivable." (Griffin's Panjab Rajas). In the fertile and populous central districts " wheat sold at from ih to 2k seers for the
"rupee, the people fled to Hindustani, Kashmir, and Peshawar, the seeds of the acacia and the cotton plant were greedily devoured,
"so many died of starvation that bodies were thrown into the wells unburied, mothers cast their children into the rivers, and even
" cannibalism is said to have been resorted to. The cattle nearly all died, or were eaten up by the starving Mahomedans. Many
" ruins of old villages are traceable to this famine; and stories are still told of the extraordinary friendships which grew up anions
" the survivors, who clung together, sharing with each other everything available as food. The famine was followed by Teat
" mortality from fever and ague, and a large proportion of those who had escaped starvation fell victim to disease." (Saunders
and Waterjield—Lahore and, Gujrat Reports.) Even in Hazara, which has escaped untouched by the many droughts which have
since devastated the Panjab, " this famine fell with terrible severity. Grain sold at 3;V to 4^ seers per rupee, and was not to be had
" even at that price when the famine was at its height; and popular accounts describe the district as nearly depopulated." (JVace.)
         118. T h e P a n j a b f r o m 1800 A . D . t o a n n e x a t i o n . — W i t h the b e g i n n i n g of the p r e s e n t century the
e a s t e r n p a r t s of t h e Province found rest, at least from external troubles. In 1803 the t r e a t y of Sirji Anjano-am
m a d e us masters of the Dehli and Hissdr d i v i s i o n s ; a n d in 180S we confined the rising ambition of
Ranjit S i n g h to t h e country w e s t of the Satluj, and took the States of the E a s t e r n Plains, with the
exception of Kapurthala, u n d e r our p r o t e c t i o n . T h e country immediately to t h e w e s t of the Satluj also
enjoyed comparative political peace, for the s u p r e m a c y of Ranjit Singh was practically absolute. But
on the b o r d e r he gradually reduced t o nominal subjection the tribes of the t r a n s - I n d u s frontier, who had ever
been impatient of the yoke, even when imposed by one of their own race and religion ; while in the
hills he fought with the Gurkhas over t h e spoils of the a n c i e n t R a j p u t k i n g d o m s . During the first forty
y e a r s of the century six famines of g r e a t e r or less severity occurred, in 1802, 1812, 1817, 1824, 1833, and
 1837.        T h o s e of 1802, 1817, 1824, and 1837 were less fatal a n d less g e n e r a l than those of 1812 and 1S33,
a n d w e r e a p p a r e n t l y confined to the east of the Province, where in 1841 an epidemic of fever reached
such a height that " the crops died s t a n d i n g for w a n t of people to cut t h e m , " and was succeeded in the
following y e a r by a drought of considerable severity. T h e famine of 1833 was almost equal in severity
to that of 1783.
          In the eastern and south-eastern districts " it forms the epoch from which old men fix the dates of events. In many villages no
 "land was even ploughed up, in but few was any seed sown, in none was a crop reaped. What little T-ass spnunr up was eaten
 "by locusts. The cattle died, wheat rose to 8 seers per rupee, and the people followed their cattle; while crowds of emigrants from
 " the highlands to the west poured into the district to help the residents to starve " (Karndl Report). The people of "hohtak sav
 of this famine:—"The shop-keeper hid in his house, the child wept over its meal " (Fanshawe). lo the central districts the
 distress was not so severe, but " famine raged in Kashmir, and a great influx of people was. the result, most of them only to die;
 " many came to sell their children who are still (1870) to be found in tho houses of the prostitutes." (Waterfield's Gi'ijrdt Report.)
          Six years of anarchy which succeeded the death of Ranjit Singh were t e r m i n a t e d by the bloody war
 with ourselves; a n d so the Panjab passed u n d e r English rule. W h a t the s t a t e of the country was when
 it came into our hands, and w h a t the nature of the rule which was superseded by our own, I shall now
 endeavour to indicate.

    119. State of the Dehli Territory at annexation.—The districts of Dehli, Gurgaon, Rohtak, and part of
Karnal were, as already stated, acquired by us in 1803. The state of affairs to which our interference put

          " So ended in 1S05 t h a t terrible time called by t h e people t h e Sikh hurly-burly, or the J I a h r a t t a anarchy. I t s horrors still live

       Five years later Captain Abbott, Settlement Officer, described the Sikh rule in the Protected States

"oppressions, made inroads with impunity, and aggravated the general disorder. For three years this state of anarchy continued;
"in the fertile valleys of Ka"ngra not a blade of cultivation was to be seen, grass grew up in the towns, and tigresses whelped in

    The burden was too heavy to be borne, and in 1809 Ranjit Singh was called in. Under the Sikh rule
which succeeded in KAngra, the whole country was farmed out to Kdrddrs of foreign race and reli-
gion.
     " The KardaV was a judicial as well as a fiscal officer. But his fiscal duties were most important. Corrupt judgments or an in-
" sufficient police were evils which might be overlooked, even supposing that they excited attention; but a Kardar in arrears was an
"offender almost beyond the hope of pardon. The problem of his life was therefore to maintain cultivation at the highest possible
" level, and at tbe same time to keep the cultivator at the lowest point of depression. The burden of the people way as heavy as
" they could bear; the utmost limits of toleration had been attained. A native collector is too discreet to ruin his tenants ; bnt he
" will proceed to any length short of actual destruction His policy is to leave nothing hut a bare subsistence to the cultivator of
" the soil. But tbe assessment was generally equal; and the burden, heavy indeed according to just and liberal principles, TO still
"impartially distributed."     (Ibid.)
     In the hill country east of the Satluj, namely in Simla and all the Hill States except Chamba, Mandi,
and Suket, the Gurkhas held sway and horribly oppressed the people, till in 1816, after the Gurkha war,
we took the tract under our protection. The three States just mentioned, with Kulu, remained practically
independent till within a few years of our annexation of the Panjab. Mr, Lyall thus describes the rule in
Kiilu :—
     " The Rajas were petty despots in league with the priests, often cruel and avaricious, and recognising very faintly any law
" or custom; and they and their favourites did much as they liked, or as their jealousy or avarice prompted thein. A man's
" ancestral house and lands were .--"ometitnes confiscated and transferred for no fault. To seem to he well-to-do or influential was
" to be in danger. As an example, in 1862 a large sum of money was accidentally exhumed. On enquiry it appeared that it belonged
" to a family of which the women were hereditary foster-mothers to the royal family, and which had thus acquired wealth and influence.
" Three generations ago, on some slight pretext, the Raja suddenly seized the whole family and buried them all alire, men, women, and
" children, probably because the hidden treasure was not forthcoming. The only survivors were a woman and her infant, who escaped
"because the mother happened to be serving at the time as wet-nurse in the palace. The number of women burnt at a Kaja's funeral
" was often prodigious. Quite as great tyranny, however, prevailed in other petty hill states."
     There is a village on the border between Kulu and Bashahr called PandraMs or "Fifteen-twenty,"
and which was so named because neither of these two rival states could hold it for longer than 15 to 20
days at a time.
     122. Sikh rule on the Frontier.—If such was the state of affairs among the comparatively peaceable
population of the east and north of the Province, it may be imagined what was the condition of the frontier,
where wild hill tribes, still many of them semi-savage, accustomed to assert their independence even of
the Kcibul kingdom, and habitually fighting one with another for sheer love of the game, were brought under
the rule of the hated Sikh. Even Ahmad Shah—
" collected tribute by an army sent periodically to extort it at tbe sword's point;" and as the Durrani power over the frontier grew
weak, " his quondam vatssats in the Indus Provinces grew stronger, till one by one each declared himself independent and began to
"make war on his neighbour, only to fall an easy prey a few years later to the devouring Sikh. Toe present century opened with a
" general scramble for territory. Eaob group of villages was a little independent State, now warring with its neighbours, now at
" peace, now gaining and now losing territory. Might 'was right, and the general law of the land was Islam corrected by assassina-
"tion. Betweeu 1823 and 1845 the country was every second or third year invaded by a large Sikh army, which harried their|fields,
"trod down their harvests, burnt their houses, and inflicted injuries which it took the intervals of peace to repair." (Tkorbum.)
      Sir Herbert Edwardes thus describes the state of the country in 1847 : -
       " The Bannuchia are bad specimens of Afghans. Could worse be said of any human race p They have all the vices of Pathans
"rantly luxuriant, the virtues stunted. Except in Sindh I have never seen such a degraded people. They are not of pure descent
" from any common stock,bnt represent the ebb and flow of might, right, possession, and spoliation in a corner of the Kabul empire
"whose remoteness and fertility offered to outlaws and vagabonds a secure asylum against both law and labour. Let the reader
" take these people and arm them to the teeth; then, throwing them down in the beautiful country I have described, bid them
"scramble for its fat meads and fertilizing waters, its fruits and flowers ; and he will have a good idea of the state of landed pro-
"perty and laws of tenure as I found them in 1847. Owning no external allegiance, let us see what internal government this
"impatient race submitted to: in truth none. Freed from a king they could not agree upon a chief—but every village threw a mud
" wall around its limits, chose its own malih (master), and went to war with all its neighbours."
      And Mr. Thorburn says of the same parts—
       "At that time most of the bed of the Indus (now a sheet of splendid cultivation) was a jungle of trees and tiger gTass in which
"tbe sportsmen of both banks used to drive pig, hog-deer, aud other game. To contrast the difference between 1850 and 1877 in a
"few words, I may say that since the former year cultivation has more than doubled, population has increased 20 per cent.,
"7,000 nomadic and mostly pastoral "Wazrri have grown into 14,000, holding 60,000 acres of cultivated laud, and crime has fallen to
" the level of an orderly district like Shahpur, Instead of one high road of 60 miles in length, and destitute of bridges, there are uow
" 300 miles of high roads with scores of masonry bridges; and finally, instead of a restless suspicious population, there is now a quiet
"law-abiding trustful people, the great mass of which is, I honestly believe, thoroughly loyal.'
      123. In Peshawar the state of things was even worse:—
    " From 1800 to 1820 Peshawar remained in a constant state of excitement and confusion, passing from one ruler to another,
"none of whom could exercise much real control over its wild occupants, and the hill tribes transferring their allegiance to tbe
"highest bidders."
      The Sikh occupation brought no alleviation—
     " The periodical visits of the Sikhs were calamitous to the people : their approach was the signal for tbe removal of property
"and valuables and even of the window and door-frames from the houses; crowds of women and children fled frightened
"from their houses, and the country presented the appearance of an emigrating colony. As the hated host advanced they overran
"tbe neighbourhood, pillaging and destroying whatever came within their reach, and laying waste the fields. There is scarce
" a village from the head of the valley to the Indus which has not been burnt and plundered by the Sikh Commander; his visitations
" were held in such awe that his name was used by mothers as a term of affright to hush their unruly children; and at the present
" day, in travelling through the country, old grey beards with many scars point out the hills over which they were 'chased like sheep
" by tbe Singh,' and young men show where their fathers fought and fell. Destruction was so certain that the few villages which from
" the extreme difficulty of their positions were either passed by the enemy or, resisting attack, were but partially destroyed, claimed a
"triumph, and came to be looked upon as invincible.
       " But the people of this unhappy country did not enjoy peace, even during the respites which the withdrawal of the Sikhs
" afforded them; and it is hard to say whether they suffered most from those terrible but passing invasions, or from the bitter feuds
" which followed them, arising out of hostile acts committed towards each other, either to find favour from the invaders, or to
** gratify personal feelings of hatred and revenge; for, as is common with people in such a depraved condition, they had no scruple
" ra betraying each other for such purposes, and as spies or informers in bringing the Sikh scourge upou their neighbours with

       124. The state of the Cis-Indus and Salt-range Tracts.—On this side of the Indus the people were
 more peaceful;. but this only made them easier subjects of extortion.
        " A great portion of the country was farmed out to grantees who possessed judicial and executive authority within the limits of
"their grants, and were quite independent of the local officials. They were almost invariably non-residents, and put in agents.
 "known as Hakims, to manage their estates These Hakims were more or less in the habit of raiding on one another and
" lifting cattle; and the country till the time of SaVan Mai was generally in a disturbed slate." (Tucker's JJerah Ismail Report.)
       Sir Herbert Edwardes thus describes the inhabitants of the Thai or sandy plain between the Indus
and the Jahlam-Chanab as he found them at annexation:—
        "The men, stout, fierce, and fearless of man or beast, clad in shagiry cloaks of brown camel's hair, drive out the herds
" t o feed, and, with long matchlock in hand, and hurtling mutch, lie full length along the ground and listen for strange loot-

       In the Salt-range tract—
" anarchy had reigned for centuries, and from the oldest times the district had been overrun hy hordes of invaders, from Greeks to
" Afghans. They swept through it and disappeared. The temporary desolation, the plundered homes, the deserted homesteads were
 "all things of the hour, and are now forgotten. But it was the rule of the Sikh Kardars, too far off from Lahore to be under anv
"check, that reduced the Rajput and Gakkhar alike to their present state of poverty. Their rule was a military despotism, and

'• of different tribes travellers and caravans had to satisf}' the rapacity of each hy paying black mail, or they had to submit to be
"plundered, outraged, and ill treated, happy sometimes to escape with life." (Cracroft and Brundreth—Rawalpindi and Jahlam
 Reports.)
       125. The Sikh rule in the central districts.—In the centre and south-west of the Province the Sikh
 rule was stronger and more equitable. In the earlier days, indeed, previous to and during the growth
 of the misls, it was nothing better than an organised system of massacre and pillage. But as the
 Sikhs grew into a people and a national spirit developed, self-interest, if nothing higher, prompted a
 more moderate government. Still, as Sir Robert Egerton recorded, the Sikh population were soldiers
 "almost to a man," and their one object was to wring from the Hindu and Mahomedan cultivators the
 utmost farthing that could be extorted without compelling them to abandon their fields. The Rajput
 especially, who had refused to join the ranks of an organisation in which his high caste was disregarded,
 was the peculiar object of their hatred and oppression. Not to be for them was to be against them,
 and all who had any pretensions to wealth or influence were mercilessly crushed. -They promoted and
 extended cultivation as far as was possible under a system which held forth the minimum of inducement
 to the cultivator; but they acknowledged nothing higher than the husbandman, the)' respected no rights
 and they recognised no property where such respect or such recognition conflicted with their pecuniary
 interests, and he who was not a Sikh, and therefore a soldier, was only valuable in so far as he could
 be utilised as a payer of revenue. Their rule was just and even, in that they meted out oppression to all
 with an equal hand.
        The whole country was farmed out to Jat KaVdars who were responsible to the State for a certain
annual amount of revenue, and for nothing else: and beyond that amount, itself always increasing as
cultivation spread, anything that they could extract, no matter by what means, was their own. Fixity
of demand was unknown. The share of the gross produce nominally taken was one-half; but to this
were added numberless cesses. Mr. Wynyard enumerates 38 of these, of ever-varying nature and amount.
Mr. Purser says of the Sikh rates—
         " It may be as well to explain that these rates mean nothing, for if the fundamental principle of the Sikh system was that the
" Government should take as much as ever it could, as often as it could, and whenever it could, the principle that a spade should
" on no account he called a spade was only second in importance to it, and was much more rarely violated. The advantages of this
" were that the people were made to believe that great favours were being bestowed on them while they were helng taxed as
" heavily as possible, and that the subordinate officials were able to plunder the Government to their heart's content, as no one knew
" what their accounts meant. Thus a man would be charged six rupees for six kanals of cotton. The generous Kardar remitted
" half as an act of grace, and then added R4.-1-6 on account of extra cesses."
        Sir Richard T e m p l e , o n e of t h e most able apologists of the Sikh rule, finds nothing better to say of it
than that, though oppressive a n d extortionate, it w a s orderly, and " g e n e r a l l y abstained from wanton cruelty ;
t h a t it w a s n o t an unmixed evil; a n d t h a t the condition of t h e people w a s not wholly pitiable.'' O t h e r offi-
cers speak of it less favourably. Mr. P u r s e r thus describes the s t a t e of affairs in Montgomery, next door
to t h e capital of t h e P r o v i n c e —
        " The villages seem to have been farmed to the highest bidder. As might be expected from such a system, oppression flourished.
" There was very little securily either. The people had only two ways of protecting themselves, the first was to go to Lahore
 "and complain; the second was to murder the Kardar; neither was very satisfactory, as the result was only to introduce a still
"more rapacious party on the scene. The ruins of old forts are still numerous in the district. Wells used to be provided with little
"towers to which the cultivator might fly on the approach of danger. A couple of matchlocks were kept in them, and beneath
 " them was an enclosure for cattle. Thus eu'tivators carried 011 their work. Han jit Singh had a police station at Knlula, and there
 " was another belonging to Bahawnlpur at Tibbi, four miles off; yet the country was so unsettled that people semrely dated to cuts?
 " between the two if they had anything worth stealing with them. About 1S.30 Diwan Sawau Jlal obtained charge of the srreater
 " portion of the district. His rule was decidedly vigorous ; at first villages in which serious crimes took place were burnt as examples:
 " the track law was strictly enforced. He had canals dug, and by light rents and a just administration caused huge areas to be
 "brought under cultivation. The tribes of the liavi were, however, not to he weaned from evil ways in a hurry, and in 1S43 they
 " were out and plundered half the country. The Wattus of the Satluj were very little better."

     127. The Panjab under English rule.—What wonder that, when they came into our hands, Sirsa and
the Greater part of HissaV were almost uninhabited, Karnal, Rohtak, South Ambala and Firozpur, on re
covered with rich cultivation, were largely waste or jungle, and Shahpur " a n almost ruined and deserted
tra*t of country," while the now fertile valleys of the Indus and the Chanab were in many parts covered
with impenetrable forest inhabited only by wild beasts. At that time there were no canals beyond a few
inundation'channels on the Indus and Lower Satluj ; since then we have spent four and a half million sterling
on Government canals, and have encouraged the formation of some hundreds of miles of smaller irrigation
channels by private enterprise. There were then no communications worthy of the name; we now have
1 -00 miles of metalled and 23,000 of unmetalled roads, and have spent nineteen millions sterling on
Railways. In those days "the badness and insecurity of the roads and the levy of vexatious transit and
customs dues prevented exportation of grain to any distance," and the people of one district starved for
want of food while plenty reigned in parts of the Province not very far distant; there is now no import
duty save on salt, and that taken on only a single line along our western frontier. We have substituted a
fixed and moderate, if inelastic, assessment of land revenue for a demand about which the only certainty
was that it would be excessive. I quote the Administration Report for 1872-73 :—
       " The Sikhs often actually took as much as one-half the gross produce of an estate, besides a multitude of cesses : our demand
•; never exceeds oue-sixth, is frequently not more than an eighth, a tenth, or a twelfth, and in some cases not more than a fifttuiitli
" of the average gross produce, valued at average, prices for a period of 20 to 30 years."
      Above all, we have replaced murder and violence by peace and order, and the traveller now sings,
with full pockets, for the robber is in gaol. No more striking example of the effect which orderand tranquil-
lity had upon "the Province can be adduced than the fall of prices which ensued immediately upon our
ta'king the Panjab, and no better proof can be given of the development which it has undergone in our
hands than the rise which those same prices have since experienced ; for the high prices of the Sikh rule
were rendered inevitable by the discouragement which anarchy and oppression offered to production, while
the hiodi prices of the present day are rendered possible by the connection of the Panjab wheat fields with
the markets of India and of the world. I give below the average prices of wheat and gram in the Panjab
in pounds per rupee from 1841 to 1880, with five-yearly averages.

      130. Annual chronicle.—The facts and figures discussed in the preceding paragraphs will enable the
reader to estimate with some degree of accuracy the advance in prosperity and the general development
of resources which have taken place in the Pan jab since it fell into our hands. But in order to explain the
fluctuations in population which the Census figures disclose, it will be necessary to exhibit briefly the
character of the several years which have intervened between the successive enumerations. No descrip-
tion or discussion is needed ; and Abstract No. 21 below, which shows for each year the leading vital statis-
tics, the rainfall, and the price of food, and the notes appended to which sum up in a few words the naturr
of the seasons and such events as have affected the movements or increase of the population, pre-
sent in a concise and convenient form the facts to which reference will have to be made, not only in this
chapter, but still more when we come to discuss the age statistics. The vital statistics are notoriously imper-
fect; those of births more so than those of deaths, and those for the whole Province more so than those
for municipalities. The earlier figures are probably far less correct than the later ones, and especially
the earliest figures of all, when registration was in its infancy. But though the general increase in tlie
rates is largely due to improvement in registration, vet that improvement has been gradual and constant,
and sudden fluctuations in the figures are almost certainly due to actual fluctuations in the facts. The
figures at least never err by being in excess of the truth ; and as the tendency year by year is to reduce the
number of unreported births and deaths, any decrease in the rates must be real.

      131. Contrast between the two inter-Census periods.—A glance at the resume given above will
at once make evident the reason why the increase of population between 1S68 and 18S1 was not
only so much smaller than that between 1855 and 1868, but so absolutely small in itself when the pro-
gress made in other respects is taken into consideration. The most marked feature of vital statis-
tics in India is the incessant and violent fluctuations which characterise them. In England the birth
and death-rates vary from year to year by decimals per thousand: in India, by considerable percentages
of their total amount. Nor is this to be wondered at, in the Panjab at least, The population of the

But of all Northern India, the lower plains of the east of the Panjab, which include 2S percent, of the whole
population of the Province, are the portion most liable to excessive variation of season and to destructive
failure of rain. They lie on the border land between the area of fairly certain rainfall where failure is
but seldom to be apprehended, and the area of normal drought where failure is comparatively immate-
rial, as cultivation is impossible save where irrigation renders it independent of the seasons. Their rainfall

         132. Now the Census of 1855 was t a k e n exactly half-way b e t w e e n two of these periodical famines ,
a n n e x a t i o n had only p r e c e d e d it b y an interval of six y e a r s , and its effects had scareel)- had time to m a k e
