      I will discuss the male                   figures                 first.                ,
      T h e pre-eminence of the Jains is very striking, but also very natural. They consist almost wholly of
the mercantile classes, and very largely of the wealthiest portions of those classes, and indeed I am inclined
to think that the figures must be very much understated. There are out of every 10,000 Jains over 6,500
who are above 15 years of age, and a very small proportion of these can be'still at school. Yet it is
difficult to believe that more than 2,800 of them cannot read and write. It is possible that in some places,
as already suggested, only such as could read and write the Persian character were returned as educated.
At any rate whatever the nature of the error may be, I do not believe that the figures are correct ; nor do 1
believe that only 650 out of the 1,160 children between 10 and 15 years of age which are found anion" every
 10,000 Jains are under instruction.

                                                 EDUCATION IN THE PANJAB.                                                 L Chap. IX.

                                                            Education.

        The Buddhists come n e x t ; but here Mr. Anderson's qualification must b e r e m e m b e r e d that probably
very many of these men can only read and not write. The monks which almost every Spiti family contains
are taught to read in the monasteries ; but as a rule they do not learn to write also. Mr. Anderson writes
thus of education in Lahul and S p i t i : " In Lahul a comparatively large number can read and write
" Tankri, Pahari, and also Tibetan. Education is more advanced there than in Kulu. The Lamas can all read
" the printed character, but they are not all able to write Tibetan. They do not as a rule know Tankri.
" T h e traders know both'Tankri and Tibetan. The fact of the Lahulis engaging generally in trade both with
'* KiSIu and with Ladakh and Tibet, may explain why the d e m e n t s of education are more widespread among
" them than in Kulu. There is only one school in Lahul, and in it both Urdu and Tibetan are taught. Before
" b o y s are admitted into the Urdu classes they have to pass through a course in Tibetan. Still here, as in
" Kulu, education is considered a species of begar (forced labour), and the father expects to be exempted
" from carrying loads, & c , while his son is at school. In Kulu there are two schools ; but they would have
" very few scholars were not the parents encouraged by exemption from begdr to send their children. Edu-
c a t i o n in Spiti is at its lowest. Few can read and fewer still can write. Urdu is unknown, and an inter.
" preter is kept to carry out or translate for the benefit of the headmen the few orders that relate to that
" part of the sub-division. There is no school in Spiti."
       Next to them come the Hindus, and here again their comparatively high position is due to the large
proportion of them engaged in commerce, especially in the towns. The proportion of Hindus at school or
already educated steadily rises from one division to another as the generally Hindu character of the popu-
lation d e c r e a s e s ; it is lowest in Dehli and the Hill States where Hinduism is most prevalent, and highest
on the frontier where Hinduism is least general ; and this is due to the fact that wherever the general popu-
lation is Musalman, the Hindus belong almost entirely to the mercantile classes. The proportion is natu-
rally greater in the towns where commerce is most rife; and the difference between town and village is
largest in this respect where Hinduism is most common, and where therefore the largest proportion of the
rural Hindu population is agricultural.
       Next follow the Sikhs, an almost purely agricultural and artisan population, with not much more than
half the percentage for Hindus, and still less than that in the specially Sikh t r a c t s ; and here again the
same points are observable as with the Hindus, for in the parts where Sikhs are few many of them are
educated Khatris. Last of all come the Musalmans with a uniformly low proportion of educated among

 wholly illiterate, come the Hindus. But the most encouraging feature of the figures, if they are even ap-
 proximately correct, is the proportion of scholars to educated adults, which would seem to show that the
 education of women is really making progress in the new generation. There are about three times as
 many "women over 15 years of age as there are girls between 5 and 15; and even on the exaggerated
 assumption that the ordinary schooling of a native girl lasts from 5 to 15, if 8'g per 10,000 of the grown-
 up women can read and write, only 2-97 should at the same rate be under instruction. Instead of this there
 are 6-3, or more than twice as many as there should be. In other words, education is twice as general
 among the girls of 5 to 15 years of age as it is among the women of over 15 years. The figures are small
 a t the b e s t ; b u t so far as they may be trusted they show distinct progress.

      Progress is apparent, even if we omit those under instruction, in every district except Dehli, Karnal,

                                                                                 CHAPTER X.
     INSANITY, BLINDNESS, DEAF-DUMBNESS, AND
                     LEPROSY.
        816. Introductory.—At the. Census of 1881 we recorded the number of insane, blind, deaf-mutes, and
l e p e r s ; and the figures will be found in Tables XIV to XVII, Appendices A and B, classified according to
religion, age, and sex. So far as intention goes I believe the figures to be correct. Mr. Wilson writes of
Sirsa : " T h e figures for infirmities are probably almost quite correct. T h e people did not seem to try and
" conceal such cases, which were well known in the village, though of course whatever error there be is not
" o n the side of exaggeration." I believe that this was the general experience, and that intentional mis-
statement or concealment was exceedingly rare, among the male population at any rate. I do not feel quite
so certain about the figures for females. But some of the infirmities recorded are not easily defined ; and
this difficulty did no doubt lead to error in some cases, which will be indicated in treating of the respective
heads. T o discuss statistics for infirmities instructively requires special professional knowledge, in which I
am of course wholly lacking; and all I can attempt to do is to present the figures in a convenient form for
examination. Dr. Townsend, our Surgeon-General, to whom I applied for assistance, informs me that to
examine the figures thoroughly with the view of explaining the variations which they present would be a
work of great labour, and would require very special study.


                                                                                        INSANITY.
               817. Insanity in the various parts of the Panjab.—Table XIV of Appendices Aand B gives the statistics
for insanity. Here there is little room for doubt, and the figures are in all probability very fairly correct. No
doubt they include idiots and various degrees of unsoundness of mind, but this was intended. The word baivala
which was used in the vernacular instructions corresponds very fairly with " u n s o u n d mind," and includes
both the mad and the idiot. A t the same time the Civil Surgeon of Muzaffargarh points out that " there are
" m a n y beggars who pretend to be decayed in their minds, but who are really idle malingering vagabonds ;
" a n d perhaps these cases may have greatly helped to swell the total number returned as of unsound
" m i n d . " T h e observation is just, for the natives look upon the idiot with a special pity and almost with
respect. A b s t r a c t N o . 131 below shows the number of insane among every 10,000 of the population in each
district and state, and gives also the corresponding figures for 1868.

                                                                                                                             C   Chap. X.

                                                               Insanity.

The figures bring out one fact with the most startling plainness ; and that is, that insanity is most common
in the south-western districts, next most common in the hilly districts, and less frequenLKlfn extraordinary
degree in the central and eastern plains of the Panjdb. There are 23 distric{rf*j|a»states above the
average of the Province. Of these the four districts of the Multin division with CharJRfand N^han stand
highest in the list, all having 8 or more insane per 10,000 of both sexes and 10 or morj^ajpong the males.
Immediately below them comes Bah£walpur with 7 persons and 9 males ; and of the remaining 16 districts
and states above the average, every single one except Kalsia and Loharu has hills in it; while Kalsia lies
immediately at the foot of the hills, and both it and Loharu are below the average if males alone be
regarded. . On the other hand, of the 32 districts and states which are below the average, only Hushyarpur,
Bashahr, Gurdaspur, Mandi, and the petty Hill States include hills ; while every single district or state of the
centre and east of the P a n j i b is well below the average, whether females or males be taken as the standard
of comparison. If males alone be taken Bashahr rises to the average, and Hushyarpur and Mandi and the
collective minor Hill States come only just below it. Some of the smaller Hill States indeed still stand
low; but their population is exceedingly small, and their Census was probably less accurate than that of
any other part of the Province.
     818. One cause at least of this distribution of insanity is I believe well recognised. Cretinism, which
is only one form of idiocy, is always found to accompany goitre ; while goitre is known to be specially pre-
valent in the hills and in the south-western districts. W h y it shouldbe so prevalent in the south-western
districts, far removed as most of them are from any chalk formation, is apparently not so well understood.
In Jhang goitre is said to be most common in the north-east, and in Hazira in the lower portions of the dis-
trict and on the banks of the Indus. The following extracts from Colonel MacMahon's Amritsar report
and Mr. Coldstream's Hushyarpur report are interesting :—
        " Goitre is extraordinarily prevalent in some parts of the Bajwa't or tract under the Jamrau hills. I resided in the Sia"lkot
*' district as Assistant Commissioner for five years, and frequently visited Bajwat between 1856 and 1861. Nowhere in so small
" a space, not even in the worst valleys in Switzerland, have I seen so much goitre and cretinism. As these diseases show tbem-
" selves nowhere else in the Sialkot district, as they are not found in the left bank of the Chanab, and as I was told by the Maharaja's
" officials that they are not common in the low hills of Jamuru above Bajwat, their presence in Bajwat itself is in all probability
" d u e to physical causes. Bajwat is a swampy malarious tract and possibly the well water may be contaminated by injurious
" mineral matter. If I remember right, the fast view of the origin of goitre is that it is due to drinking water flowing through
" magnesious lime-stone tracts impregnated with certain mineral substances of which iron pyrites (sulphide of iron) appears to be
"considered especially injurious." {Colonel MacAfakon.)
       " Goitre or ' g i l l e r ' as the natives call it, is very prevalent in the villages of Dodial, Rampur, and Budhabar, and it is also
" known in Sehowra. These are all villages situated in, or near to the base of the hills. The most intelligent natives with whom
" I have conversed on the point attribute the disease to drinking the water of the ravines or " kliails" as they are locally termed, and
" it seems far most common, if not exclusively found in villages of which the inhabitants drink ravine water and not well water. No
" doubt in Switzerland and Derbyshire also the people drink largely of the water of mountain streams, so possibly the disease in all
" these places may be attributed to this one common proximate cause. What the particular element in this kind of water may be
*' must be left to time and physiological science to decide. I have on a previous occasion made an estimate that 5 to 10 per cent.
" of those afflicted with goitre will be probably found more or less imbecile. The affliction is much more common in the Trans-
" Beds Kangra district than it is here; so common indeed that when a betrothal is arranged with a bride of that quarter, there is
" always an inquiry made as to whether or not she is affected with goitre." {Mr. Coldstream.)
       T h e r e is another possible cause of insanity in the western half of the Panjafj, and that is the custom
of marrying near relations which is there prevalent. In the eastern half of the Province, marriage even
within the clan is absolutely forbidden by tribal custom to the mass of the population whatever may be
their religion. But among the Mahomedans of the west the prohibition is not so general, and among the
higher classes at least marriage of cousins is common. Whether this close breeding has really any share
in accounting for the larger proportion of insane in the western districts, is a question for further examin-
ation bylthe light of professional knowledge.
       819. Figures for insanity compared with t h o s e of last Census.—The figures of 1868 and 1881 given
side by side in the Abstract above compare curiously. On the whole the proportion of insane is shown to have
increased, and most largely in those parts where insanity now appears to be most prevalent, our figures
often showing a decrease in the Eastern Plains. I suspect that the difference is chiefly due to greater
accuracy of enumeration. T h e system of the last Census, at which the only question asked was, " H a v e
 " y o u any idiots in your house, and if so, how m a n y ? " was especially likely to lead to omissions; which
are much less probable when the specific question is asked regarding each separate person, as it was on
 the present occasion, " I s he of sound mind, or i n s a n e ? " The increase is largest in the hilly and
 frontier districts where we have already seen reason to believe that the Census of 1868 was least accurate.
 As regards females, I suspect that our figures are still somewhat in defect of the truth, and that those of 1868
 were far more so. If the present figures are correct the proportion of insane is, in every single case
 except Kalsia and Loharu, markedly smaller among females than among males ; and this is, I believe,
 exactly opposed to the experience of other countries.

                                                                                        Blindness.

      I have added the distribution by age of total population in columns 2, 5, 7, and 10, so that the distri-
bution by age of total insane in columns, 3, 4, 8, and 9 may be compared with it. The above figures show
how comparatively rare insanity is before 10 years of age in both sexes, and how largely it appears to
develop between 15 and 20 in the case of males and between 10 and 15 in the case of females, which are
about the period at which marriage, in the sense of cohabitation, takes place among the two sexes respec-
tively. Also how shortlived the insane appears tb be in comparison with the sane, though the discre-
pancy is greater in the case of females than in that of males. On the other hand, the figures for female
insanity show a sudden increase as compared with those for males after 40 years of age, the critical period
in female life. The figures of Abstract No. 133 seem to show that insanity appears earlier in life in the
western than in the eastern and central divisions ; and the similarity of the figures for males and females
in this respect give some reason for believing that this is really the case. But the figures are too small lor
it to be possible to lay any great stress upon them.

     822. Blindness in various parts Of t h e Panjab.—Table XV of Appendices A and B gives the statistics
for blindness. H c e again thefiguresare probably accurate. Perhaps some of those returned as blind were
not absolutely deprived of sight, but no other cause of error suggests itself as probable ; and it is possible
that there was less tendency to conceal the blindness of females than there may have been to conceal their
insanity. There is not much fear of those blind of one eye only having been included, as the vernacular
word tor persons so afflicted is different from that used for those blind of both eyes. Abstract Xo. 134
below shows the number of blind among every 10,000 of the population in each district and state, and gives

         23   Multan        . .        .    .     50            48         68    52       61        20   Baikal             .    .      .   .     5            9 1 .

Here again the order in which the districts and states stand in the list is very significant. All the dis-
tricts whose area consists of open plains, often s.andy, over which the dust-laden hot winds of the Panjab
sweep with unbroken violence and the dancing air seems to blaze with the glare reflected from the ground,
stand at the head of the list; while all the hilly districts in which rainfall is heavy and tree-clad mountains
subdue the glare and render dust-storms impossible, stand at the bottom. The only exceptions are Hushv-
irpur and Gurdaspur which stand high, and Multan, Jfnd, and Bahiwalpur which stand low. In the last
three irrigation is extensive, while in Hushyarpur at least there is much sand. Now blindness in the Panja*b
is generally due either to small-pox or to ophthalmia, and of the two ophthalmia is by very much the more
frequent cause 1 ; and dust, heat and glare cause ophthalmia 2 . It is curious that the proportion of blind
should be so much larger among females than among males, and that in almost every district in the
      * There were in the year 1881 no fewer than 91,000 cases of ophthalmia admitted to Our hospitals, or nearly as ninny as the total
number of blind persons in British Territory ; and in Kohat no less than one-third of the whole admissions to the dispensary in ISSQ were
on this account.
      • The natives commonly attribute blindness to the eating of frumenty made of bijra. Nuw bajra is sown only in sandy soil.

                                                                                                            Blindness.

Province. One would think that men were, as leading a more exposed life, more likely than women to suffer,
from ophthalmia. Chetan Shah, Civil Surgeon of Jhang, says that women suffer far more than men from
 inverted eyelashes, a common cause of blindness; and he accounts for their more often losing their sight,
by their being exposed to the smoke and heat of the fires over which they cook their food. But if this
were the cause, the proportion of blind among women should vary much less than that among men, and
should not follow the same order of magnitude as the figures for males. The Abstract however shows that
the fluctuation is even g r e a t e r among females than among males, while the order of districts is much the
same in both cases.
     823. F i g u r e s for blindness compared with those of last Census.—The decrease of blindness among
males since last Census is most marked. It appears in 29 out of the 32 districts, and in many is very
large indeed. T h e spread of vaccination' and the greater facilities now afforded for medical treatment,
combined with the extraordinary faith the natives place in our operation for cataract and the eagerness
with which they submit themselves to it, probably account for a great part of the decrease. Among females
the decrease is not so well m a r k e d ; and the reluctance which natives feel to bring their women to our dis-
pensaries, or to allow operations to be performed upon them, p e r h a p s explains the difference.

      N O T E . — T h i s table m a y be read t h u s : O u t of every 1,000 males 121 (col. 2) a r e between 10 a n d 15 years of a g e . Out of every 1,000 blind
males 53 (col. 3) a r e of t h a t a g e . O u t of every 1,000 females 105 (col. 5) a r e of t h a t a g e . Out of every 1,000 blind females 38 (col. 4) are of that a e e
O u t of every 1,000 males 640 (col. 7) a r e under 30 years old. Out of every 1,000 blind males 273 (col. 8) a r e under 30 years of a g e , and so forth.

      The late stage of life at which blindness develops is very marked, more especially among females
and the figures for the several divisions exhibit a wonderful uniformity in this respect. Blindness in early
life seems to be far more rare among females than among males ; but after 40 years of age the proportion
changes. T h e figures would appear to show that more than half the living blind are over 50 years of age.

                                                                                   DEAF-DUMBNESS.
      826. Deaf-dumbness in-various parts of t h e Panjab—Table XVI of Appendices A and B gives statis-
tics for the deaf and dumb. Enumerators were instructed to enter " o n l y those who have been both
" deaf and dumb from birth." T h e congenital nature of the affliction was perhaps not too carefully in-
quired into. But as the heading of the column was "deaf-dumb," it is to be hoped that those who were
deaf only were seldom included ; and I believe that dumbness other than congenital is not common
T h e examination of- the figures made in section 829 shows that the statistics may be accepted as really
including, as a rule at least, only the congenitally deaf and dumb. Abstract No. 137 below mves the
number of deaf and dumb among every 10,000 of the population in each district and state. Unfortu-
nately at the Census of 1868 those who were deaf and those who were dumb were recorded separately and
there is nothing to show whether those who were both deaf and dumb were included in both column's or
not. But as the dumb are I believe almost universally deaf, I have taken the figures for the dumb as cor
responding with those for deaf and dumb, and have given them by the side of my figures in columns 5 and
7, showing the figures for the deaf separately in columns 8 and 9.—

                                                                             Deaf-Dumbness.

Here again it is extraordinary how high the hilly and sub-montane states and districts stand.           The
only ones among them that are not above the average of the Province are Jahlam, Kohat, Bhajji, and
Hazara; and in most of tbem the figures are enormously high. Of the plains districts, Shahpur, Jhang,
Muzaffargarh and Multan stand highest, while the Dehli division, Kapurthala, Firozpur with Faridkot,
Peshawar and Hissar come lowest. The central districts stand i n the middle of the list; but the
difference between the average and the lowest figures is as nothing compared with those between the
average and the highest. The proportion of deaf mutes among males is on the whole half as high again as
among females, and this disproportion is observable in every single district and state. It is just possible
that the male are less correct than the female figures; but I know no reason for suspecting that such is the
case, and I believe that the figures represent an actual fact.
      827. Figures for deaf-dumbness compared with those of last Census.—Dr. Bellew, who kindly
examined these figures for me, compares the number now returned as deaf and dumb with the total of the
separate returns of 1868 for deaf and for dumb. This comparison shows a very considerable decrease,
and he w r i t e s : —
"The decrease has been in both sexes of the population, and clearly indicates that causes are at work which are diminishing
"the extent of deaf-dumbness in this country. This infirmity,it must be remembered, is confined chiefly to the poorer classes win.,
"when prostrated with fever or any other sickness, are unable through poverty to procure for themselves the most simple and
"inexpensive of remedies; but now that aid is being given to them by the medical authorities, and greater attention paid to the
"sanitary condition of their towns and villages, it is probable that this infirmity wilf continue to decrease in a still more marked
"degree."
I am not quite satisfied however that the comparison is a just one. I suspect that the column in the
tables for 1868 headed " d e a f " included many persons who were not dumb, and that our figures should
more properly be compared with those only of the column headed " dumb." If this be done our figures
show an increase of more than 50 per cent, among males and more than 100 per cent, among females.
The meaning of the figures of last Census is so uncertain that it is not worth while to go into the compari-
son more closely.

     N O T E . — T h i s table may be read thus: Out of every 1,000males 121 (col. 2) a r e between 10 and 15 years of atre. Out of every 1.000 deaf and
dumb males 140 (col. 3) arc of that a g e . Out of every 1,000 females 105 (col. 5) a r e of t h a t arje, Out of every i^ooo deaf and d u m b temales 1; -,
(col. 4) are of that a g e . Out of every 1,000 males 640 (col. 7) are under 30 years old. Out of every 1,000 deaf and d u m b males 5y y (col. el a r e
under 30 years of age, and so forth.

Now here we have at once a test which will show us how far our figures really include only congenital
deaf-mutes. If they include none but those who were deaf and dumb from birth, the percentages of the
deaf and dumb population for each age will vary from those for total population, only by such inconsiderable
differences as might be caused by diversity in the respective death-rales of the two populations ; and if, as it
is fair to suppose, a native can hardly tell whether a child is deaf and dumb during the first few years of his
life, yet the question must be solved at least by the time the child is 10 years old ; so that the omission of
deaf-mutes under 10 years of age should make the percentages for higher ages in columns 3 and 4 some-
what higher than they ought to be. Now considering the vague nature of the native ideas of age, I think
the correspondence between the two sets of figures for age and deaf-dumbness in columns 2, ^, 4
and 5 of the table above is little short of extraordinary. T h e number of deaf-mutes for under c, vears is
much too small, and that for males between 5 and 10 a little too small; and this is due to the omission of
young children whom their parents were unwilling to set down in their own minds as permanently deaf
and dumb while there was yet a hope of their speaking. And this omission raises all the other deaf and
dumb percentages unduly. T h e correspondence is, as 1 say, very striking, and proves most clearly that
we have succeeded almost entirely in excluding the merely deaf from our tables. The percentages for the
last period of life are too high ; and it is probable that a few old people who have grown hard of hearing
from sheer a g e have been included; but the proportion they bear to the total number is wholly insigni-
ficant.

 T h e order of districts is very marked. W e have, almost without a break, first the hills, then the sub-
 montane districts, then the Eastern Plains, and last of all the Western Plains. 1 do not know what doctors
 assign as the cause of leprosy. But there is one idea suggested to me by the order of the districts, w hieh
 would be easily tested by classification of known cases of leprosy according to caste. The districts are
 roughly speaking arranged in this list in order, with respect to the number of the carrion-eating castes among
 the population. Is it possible that the feeding on dead animals and such beasts as jackals and foxes has
 anything to do with the disease ? I believe that syphilis is sometimes assigned as the cause of leprosv, and
 this would explain the high place that the Hill districts hold in the list. But if this were the true cause we
 should expect to find more lepers among the Musalma'ns than among the Hindus, the former being marked-
 ly more addicted to venery than the latter, and far m'ore in the towns than in the villages ; whereas
 exactly the reverse is the case. If my suggestion be correct both facts would bo explained, as the out-
 cast classes have for the most part been classed as Hindu,-and they are not only more numerous in the
 villages than in the towns, but eat carrion more largely in the former than in the latter. Ot course it may
 be the poverty and dirt in which these people live, rather than the nature of their food, that produces
 leprosy, if it be true, as 1 understand it is, that lepers generally belong to the lowest classes. The propor-
 tion of lepers is more than two and a half times as great among males as among females, and the dispro-
  portion is constant throughout the list; and this would appear to point to syphilis as the more probable
  explanation.
           831. Figures for leprosy compared with those of last Census.—The figures show a verv large
  decrease since 1868, both among males and among females, and the decrease is observable in everv district.

       This table may be read thus:' Out of every 1,000 males 121 (col. 2) are between 10 and 15 years of age. Out of every 1,000 lep-
rous males 28 (col. 3) are of that age. Out of every 1,000 females 105 (col. 5) arc of that age. Out of every 1,000 leprous females 38

     The figures show very clearly that leprosy is almost unknown in the earlier stages of life, that it
seldom develops before 20 years of age, and generally very much later. It does not appear to shorten life so
far as we can judge from these figures. Nearly a third of the whole lepers of either sex are returned as over
50 years old. The figures for the Multdn and DerajSt divisions however form striking exceptions to this
general rule.
